entries.short: A professional check-up of how your home uses and loses energy, with tests and a written, ranked list of upgrades.
entries.body: An energy advisor or auditor inspects the attic, walls, basement, windows, heating and cooling equipment and water heater, and usually runs a blower door test to measure air leaks. Many also use infrared (thermal) imaging and check fuel-burning appliances with a combustion safety test. You get a report showing where energy is wasted and which upgrades are worth doing first.
entries.whyItMatters: Many rebate programs require an audit before and after the work, and the results show which upgrades will actually pay off in your house instead of guessing.

values.label: Time on site (DOE)
values.value: About an hour for a basic walk-through; about four hours for a thorough assessment with diagnostic tests

values.label: Ontario HRSP assessment rebate
values.value: $600 toward the initial and follow-up assessments (assessment stream, 2+ qualifying upgrades)

entries.caNote: The official Canadian version is the EnerGuide home evaluation, done by a registered energy advisor through an NRCan-licensed service organization. Programs that use it need a pre-retrofit evaluation before work and a post-retrofit evaluation after.
entries.usNote: DOE calls it a home energy assessment. Auditors may hold BPI certification or be RESNET HERS raters. The 25C tax credit that covered part of an audit's cost ended with the 2025 tax year.

entries.short: A test that uses a powerful, calibrated fan in an outside doorway to pull air out of the house and measure how leaky it is.
entries.body: The auditor seals the fan into an exterior door frame and lowers the indoor air pressure, so outside air rushes in through every crack and gap. The fan's airflow at a standard pressure of 50 pascals (see 50 Pa) gives the home's leakage as CFM50 or ACH50. While the fan runs, the auditor can find leaks with a smoke pencil or infrared (thermal) imaging, and a repeat test after air sealing shows how much was fixed.
entries.whyItMatters: It turns 'my house feels drafty' into a number you can compare and set targets for, and it helps size heating and cooling equipment and decide whether the home needs mechanical ventilation.

values.label: Standard test pressure
values.value: 50 Pa (about 0.2 inch of water column)

entries.caNote: Canadian EnerGuide evaluations usually include a blower door test. NRCan's R-2000 Standard measures airtightness using the CAN/CGSB-149.10 method.
entries.usNote: Where a state has adopted the 2012 or newer IECC, new homes must pass a blower door test. Raters use procedures such as ANSI/RESNET/ICC 380.

aka: air changes per hour at 50 Pa

entries.short: An airtightness score: how many times an hour the house's whole volume of air leaks out while a test fan pulls on it; lower means tighter.
entries.body: ACH50 takes the leakage measured in a blower door test (CFM50) and divides it by the size of the house, so big and small homes can be compared fairly. It's calculated as CFM50 × 60 ÷ house volume in cubic feet. An ACH50 of 3 means the fan pulled out three houses' worth of air per hour at test pressure; on a normal day the house leaks far less.
entries.whyItMatters: It is the main airtightness score used by energy codes and programs, and comparing before-and-after ACH50 shows whether air sealing worked.

entries.short: The raw air-leakage result of a house's fan test: how many cubic feet of air per minute the fan must move to hold the house at test pressure.
entries.body: During a blower door test the fan's airflow at 50 pascals (see 50 Pa) is recorded as CFM50. A bigger number means more leakage, but bigger houses naturally leak more, so it's usually converted to ACH50 for comparisons. Comparing CFM50 before and after air sealing shows how much leakage the work removed.
entries.whyItMatters: It's the measurement that ACH50 is calculated from and the number that feeds the energy model behind your audit report.

entries.short: A small unit of air pressure; airtightness tests hold a house at 50 pascals, about 1/2,000 of normal air pressure, so results can be compared.
entries.body: A pascal is a very small amount of pressure, so building pressures are read with a sensitive gauge called a manometer. Testing every house at the same 50 Pa difference makes leakage results (CFM50 and ACH50) comparable from home to home. Duct leakage tests use 25 Pa, and combustion safety checks look at pressure changes of just a few pascals.
entries.whyItMatters: Pressure readings show the auditor how hard air is being pushed through leaks and whether exhaust fans could pull combustion gases back down a chimney (see depressurization).

values.label: 50 Pa in US units
values.value: About 0.20 inch of water column (1 in. w.c. at 60°F = 248.84 Pa)

values.label: For scale
values.value: Standard air pressure is 101,325 Pa, so 50 Pa is about 1/2,000 of it

entries.usNote: US gauges and HVAC specifications often use inches of water column (in. w.c.) instead of pascals.

entries.short: Uncontrolled air moving in and out of a house through cracks and gaps, carrying heat, moisture and outdoor pollutants with it.
entries.body: Air leaks in through some gaps in the building envelope (infiltration) and out through others (exfiltration), pushed by wind, the stack effect and exhaust fans. Common leak spots include attic hatches, plumbing and wiring holes, recessed lights, the rim joist (header), window and door frames, outlets and fireplace dampers. It's measured with a blower door test.
entries.whyItMatters: NRCan says uncontrolled airflow can be the major source of heat loss, and leaks that carry humid indoor air into walls and attics cause condensation, mould and ice dams.
entries.whyUs: Sealing air leaks typically cuts heating and cooling bills by 10%–20% (DOE), and air moving through walls and attics carries moisture that can cause condensation, mold and, in cold climates, ice dams.

values.label: Moisture carried by air vs. diffusion
values.value: One small air leak can carry about 100 times more moisture than diffusion through materials

values.label: Typical savings from sealing leaks (DOE estimate)
values.value: 10%–20% of heating and cooling bills

entries.short: Blocking the hidden gaps where air leaks in and out of a house, which cuts drafts, heating and cooling costs, and moisture problems.
entries.body: Air sealing uses caulking, spray foam, gaskets, weatherstripping and rigid materials to close leaks, starting with the biggest ones in the attic and basement (see attic bypass and rim joist). A blower door test before and after shows how much leakage was removed. It's normally done before adding insulation, because insulation alone doesn't stop air movement.
entries.whyItMatters: It cuts drafts, heating bills and moisture damage, but a much tighter house may need mechanical ventilation (an HRV or ERV) and a combustion safety test to keep air healthy and appliances venting properly.

values.label: DOE estimate of savings
values.value: 10%–20% on heating and cooling bills

values.label: Average leakage reduction from retrofits
values.value: 20%–30% (LBNL analysis of about 134,000 US home tests, 2012)

values.label: Ontario HRSP air sealing rebate
values.value: Up to $250 (assessment stream, 2+ upgrades)

entries.caNote: NRCan warns that stuffing batt insulation into gaps, such as at the basement header, doesn't stop air leaks; use sealants and rigid materials instead.
entries.usNote: Under DOE's May 2026 HEEHR rules, homes must generally use rebates for insulation and air sealing before heating and cooling upgrades, unless they already meet a state-set level.

entries.short: Warm indoor air rises and escapes near the top of a house, pulling cold outside air in near the bottom; it's strongest on cold days.
entries.body: Warm air is lighter than cold air, so in winter it pushes out through leaks in upper floors and the attic while replacement air is drawn in through the basement and lower floors, including the rim joist area. The bigger the indoor-outdoor temperature difference, the taller the house and the leakier it is, the stronger the effect.
entries.whyItMatters: It explains why sealing the attic and basement matters most, why upper floors feel stuffy and lower floors drafty, and why radon tends to be higher in the colder months.

entries.short: When more air is being pushed out of a house than is coming in, so the inside sits at slightly lower pressure than outdoors.
entries.body: Exhaust fans, clothes dryers, range hoods, fireplaces and chimneys all remove air, and in a tight house the replacement air has to come from somewhere, sometimes down a chimney or flue. A blower door test depressurizes the house on purpose to measure leaks; in everyday life, depressurization is what can cause backdrafting of fuel-burning appliances.
entries.whyItMatters: Auditors check it during a combustion safety test because it can pull carbon monoxide into living space, and the same pressure difference can draw soil gases such as radon indoors.

entries.short: Using a heat-sensing camera to show warm and cold spots on walls and ceilings, revealing missing insulation and air leaks.
entries.body: An infrared camera shows surface temperatures as colours, so cold streaks around a window or a dark patch on a ceiling can point to air leaks, missing insulation or wet materials. Scans work best when it's much colder (or hotter) outside than inside and are often done while a blower door test exaggerates the leaks. The camera shows symptoms; the auditor still has to confirm the cause.
entries.bodyUs: An infrared camera shows surface temperatures as colors, so cold streaks around a window or a dark patch on a ceiling can point to air leaks, missing insulation or wet materials. Scans work best when it's much colder (or hotter) outside than inside and are often done while a blower door test exaggerates the leaks. The camera shows symptoms; the auditor still has to confirm the cause.
entries.whyItMatters: It pinpoints where to air seal and insulate, and it lets you check that a contractor's work actually filled the gaps.

entries.short: Heat taking a shortcut through materials that insulate poorly, like wood studs, steel or concrete, running from the warm side to the cold side.
entries.body: Insulation fills the spaces between studs and joists, but the framing itself conducts heat much faster, creating lines of heat loss you can often see on an infrared (thermal) image. Concrete balconies, steel beams and the webs of concrete blocks act the same way. Continuous insulation over the framing, or a thermal break, interrupts the bridge.
entries.whyItMatters: Thermal bridges make a wall perform worse than the R-value on the insulation label suggests, and the cold spots they create can collect condensation and mould.
entries.whyUs: Thermal bridges make a wall perform worse than the R-value on the insulation label suggests, and the cold spots they create can collect condensation and mold.

values.label: Share of a typical wood-frame wall that is framing
values.value: Nearly one-quarter of the wall area

values.label: Walls' share of house heat loss (NRCan)
values.value: About 20%

entries.short: A test that pressurizes your heating and cooling ducts with a calibrated fan to measure how much air escapes through leaks.
entries.body: The tester seals the supply and return registers, connects a calibrated fan (often called a duct blaster) and holds the ducts at 25 pascals. The airflow needed to hold that pressure is the leakage, reported as CFM25. Total leakage counts every leak; a second version, leakage to outside, counts only air lost to attics, crawlspaces, garages or outdoors.
entries.whyItMatters: Leaky ducts waste heating and cooling you've paid for and can pull dusty or humid air from attics and crawlspaces into the house, so duct sealing is often a high-ranked audit recommendation.

values.label: Typical loss in US homes (ENERGY STAR)
values.value: About 20%–30% of the air moving through the duct system

values.label: US energy code, new homes (2021 IECC)
values.value: Total leakage 4 CFM25 or less per 100 ft² of conditioned floor area, or 3 if tested at rough-in without the air handler

values.label: ENERGY STAR new homes (Version 3)
values.value: Rough-in ≤ 4 CFM25 per 100 ft² or 40 CFM25; final ≤ 8 CFM25 per 100 ft² or 80 CFM25, whichever is greater

entries.usNote: ENERGY STAR lists ducts located in an attic, crawlspace or garage as a warning sign of duct problems, and recommends sealing with mastic or metal tape, never duct tape.

entries.short: The part of duct leakage that escapes outside the heated and cooled space, into attics, crawlspaces, garages or outdoors.
entries.body: To isolate it, the tester runs a blower door to bring the house to the same 25 pascals as the ducts, so leaks into the living space stop counting. What's left is heated or cooled air being dumped where it does no good. Ducts entirely inside the conditioned space have little leakage to outside even when they leak.
entries.whyItMatters: This is the duct leakage that directly wastes energy, so it's the better number for judging whether duct sealing will pay off.

values.label: Test setup
values.value: House and ducts both held at 25 Pa (within ±0.5 Pa of each other)

entries.short: A check that furnaces, boilers, water heaters and stoves burn cleanly and vent their exhaust outside, even with fans running.
entries.body: The auditor measures carbon monoxide (CO) in the flue and in the room, checks the draft in the chimney or vent and looks for spillage or backdrafting. The toughest version, a worst-case depressurization test, turns on exhaust fans and closes doors to see if venting still works. It's done before and after air sealing because a tighter house leaves less air for fuel-burning appliances.
entries.whyItMatters: It protects your household from carbon monoxide, and a failed test becomes a must-fix item ahead of any energy upgrade.

values.label: Health Canada indoor CO limits
values.value: 25 ppm (1-hour average); 10 ppm (24-hour average)

values.label: US EPA outdoor CO standard (NAAQS)
values.value: 9 ppm (8-hour average); 35 ppm (1-hour average)

values.label: Typical CO in US homes without gas stoves (EPA)

entries.caNote: If a problem is found, repairs to gas appliances and venting should be done by a licensed gas technician.
entries.usNote: Many US auditors follow test procedures and pass/fail limits in BPI's ANSI/BPI-1200 standard.

entries.short: The room or area holding a fuel-burning appliance such as a furnace, boiler or water heater; it's the focus of combustion safety testing.
entries.body: The CAZ is usually a basement, utility room, closet or garage. Auditors measure the air pressure there compared with outdoors, check carbon monoxide levels and test each appliance's draft, because the pressure in this space decides whether exhaust goes up the chimney or back into the house.
entries.whyItMatters: Air sealing, a new exhaust fan or simply closing the furnace-room door can change CAZ pressure enough to cause backdrafting, so it's tested before and after work.

entries.short: When exhaust from a furnace, boiler, water heater or fireplace comes back into the house instead of going up the chimney or vent.
entries.body: Spillage is exhaust escaping at the appliance, often briefly at start-up; backdrafting is a sustained reversal where the chimney pulls outside air down. Both are usually caused by depressurization from exhaust fans or by a blocked, cold or poorly sized chimney. Natural-draft appliances with a draft hood are most at risk; sealed-combustion units that take air directly from outside are designed to avoid it.
entries.whyItMatters: Exhaust contains carbon monoxide, so auditors test for this in a combustion safety test and won't recommend tightening a house until venting is safe.

entries.short: A combustion safety check run with exhaust fans on and doors set to create the lowest pressure the furnace room is likely to see.
entries.body: The auditor closes windows and exterior doors, turns on exhaust fans, the dryer and sometimes the furnace blower, and sets interior doors to make the combustion appliance zone (CAZ) as depressurized as possible. Each appliance is then fired to check its draft, spillage and carbon monoxide. If venting fails only under these conditions, fixes can include make-up air, smaller exhaust fans or replacing natural-draft appliances.
entries.whyItMatters: It reveals backdrafting risks that a normal check would miss, which is why it's done before and after major air sealing.
entries.usNote: Pass limits depend on how the appliance is vented and on the standard used, such as BPI-1200 or RESNET's CAZ procedure.

entries.short: A colourless, odourless gas from incomplete burning of fuel; it reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen and can kill at high levels.
entries.shortUs: A colorless, odorless gas from incomplete burning of fuel; it reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen and can kill at high levels.
entries.body: Furnaces, boilers, water heaters, gas stoves, fireplaces, wood stoves, generators and cars in attached garages can all produce CO. Levels are measured in parts per million (ppm) with a CO meter or alarm. Because you can't see or smell it, working CO alarms near sleeping areas are the main everyday defence.
entries.bodyUs: Furnaces, boilers, water heaters, gas stoves, fireplaces, wood stoves, generators and cars in attached garages can all produce CO. Levels are measured in parts per million (ppm) with a CO meter or alarm. Because you can't see or smell it, working CO alarms near sleeping areas are the main everyday defense.
entries.whyItMatters: Measuring CO is a core part of a combustion safety test, and air sealing or new exhaust fans can turn a marginal appliance into a dangerous one.

values.label: Typical US homes (EPA)
values.value: 0.5–5 ppm without gas stoves; often 5–15 ppm near properly adjusted gas stoves; 30 ppm or more near poorly adjusted ones

values.label: US EPA outdoor air standard (NAAQS)

entries.caNote: Health Canada recommends at least one working certified CO alarm next to sleeping areas, and smoke and CO alarms on every floor.
entries.usNote: EPA's outdoor standards are often used as a yardstick indoors; state rules on CO alarms vary.

entries.short: A way to express tiny concentrations: 1 ppm is one part of a gas in a million parts of air, used for carbon monoxide readings.
entries.body: Gas detectors report carbon monoxide (CO) and some other indoor pollutants in ppm; ppb (parts per billion) is a thousand times smaller and is used for gases like formaldehyde. Because the numbers are small, what matters is comparing a reading with a guideline and how long the exposure lasts.
entries.whyItMatters: Knowing the unit lets you read a CO meter or air quality report and tell a normal reading from a dangerous one.

values.value: 10 ppm = 0.001% of the air; 1 ppm = 1,000 ppb

values.value: 10 ppm

values.label: US EPA outdoor CO standard (8-hour average)

values.label: Health Canada formaldehyde guideline (8-hour average)

entries.short: The upward pull in a chimney or vent that carries exhaust out of the house; weak or reversed draft lets combustion gases spill indoors.
entries.body: Hot exhaust rises, creating a slight suction in the chimney that draws gases up and out. Auditors check draft with a pressure gauge or by holding a smoke pencil at the appliance's draft hood to see whether smoke is pulled in. Draft is weakest when the chimney is cold, blocked or oversized, or when the house is depressurized.
entries.whyItMatters: Poor draft can lead to backdrafting and carbon monoxide in the house, so it's checked during every combustion safety test.

entries.short: Canada's official home energy audit: a registered energy advisor inspects and tests your home, then gives you an EnerGuide rating and an upgrade report.
entries.body: You book through a service organization, and an energy advisor registered with NRCan measures the house, records the insulation, windows, doors, and heating, cooling, hot water and ventilation equipment, and runs a blower door test. The data go into NRCan's HOT2000 software to produce your EnerGuide rating and label and a report of recommended upgrades. Programs that pay for upgrades often require one evaluation before the work and another after.
entries.whyItMatters: Many rebate programs and some city loans, such as Toronto's HELP, need an evaluation before any work starts, so book it first.

values.label: What the advisor records (NRCan)
values.value: Insulation levels, windows and exterior doors, heating, cooling and water heating equipment, ventilation, and airtightness from a blower door test

entries.short: A precise pressure gauge auditors use to read small pressure differences, in pascals, during blower door, duct leakage and combustion safety tests.
entries.body: During a blower door test one channel of the manometer reads the pressure difference between inside and outside, and another reads the fan's pressure, which converts to airflow in cubic feet per minute. Testing guidance calls for gauges accurate to about half a pascal. The same tool measures depressurization in the furnace room during a combustion safety check.
entries.whyItMatters: Accurate pressure readings are what make blower door and duct test results trustworthy and repeatable.

values.label: Accuracy (DOE Building America)
values.value: Accurate to 0.5 Pa with 0.1 Pa resolution for airtightness testing

entries.short: Everything that separates inside from outside — foundation, walls, windows, doors and roof — and controls heat, air and moisture flow.
entries.body: A good envelope has continuous insulation to slow heat, an air barrier to stop air leakage, and the right vapour control and drainage to manage moisture. Weak spots include the attic, rim joist, windows and anywhere pipes, wires or ducts pass through. Audits assess it with a blower door test, infrared (thermal) imaging and an insulation inspection.
entries.bodyUs: A good envelope has continuous insulation to slow heat, an air barrier to stop air leakage, and the right vapor control and drainage to manage moisture. Weak spots include the attic, rim joist, windows and anywhere pipes, wires or ducts pass through. Audits assess it with a blower door test, infrared (thermal) imaging and an insulation inspection.
entries.whyItMatters: Fixing the envelope first lowers heating and cooling needs, which can let you buy smaller, cheaper equipment, and some programs now require it before paying for a heat pump.
entries.usNote: DOE's May 2026 HEEHR rules require insulation and air sealing before rebated heating and cooling upgrades, unless the home already meets a state-set level.

entries.short: How well a material resists heat flow; higher is better, and insulation is rated with it, such as R-20 for walls or R-50 for attics.
entries.body: R-value measures resistance to conducted heat. Thicker insulation has a higher R-value, and materials differ in R per inch (see blown-in insulation, spray foam and rigid foam). Real performance is lower when insulation is compressed, has gaps or is bypassed by air leakage or thermal bridging.
entries.whyItMatters: Auditors compare your insulation with recommended or code levels to decide where more will pay off; attics are often the easiest place to add a lot.

entries.short: The metric version of R-value used in Canada; multiply RSI by 5.678 to get R, so RSI 8.8 is about R-50.
entries.body: RSI measures the same thing as R-value, resistance to heat flow, but in metric units (square metre kelvins per watt). Canadian building codes, product labels and EnerGuide reports often give RSI first. Because the numbers are smaller, RSI 3.5 can sound weak, but it's about R-20.
entries.whyItMatters: Converting your existing RSI and the recommended level into the same units tells you how much insulation to add.

entries.short: How fast heat passes through a window, door or wall assembly; lower is better, the opposite of R-value.
entries.body: U-factor is the rate of heat flow through a whole product, such as a window including its frame and edges. It's roughly the inverse of total R-value, so a lower number means better insulation. Compare whole-window ratings rather than centre-of-glass numbers, which look better because they leave out the frame.
entries.bodyUs: U-factor is the rate of heat flow through a whole product, such as a window including its frame and edges. It's roughly the inverse of total R-value, so a lower number means better insulation. Compare whole-window ratings rather than center-of-glass numbers, which look better because they leave out the frame.
entries.whyItMatters: Windows and doors are often the weakest part of the building envelope, so U-factor is the key number when deciding whether replacement is worth it and checking rebate eligibility.

entries.short: The share of the sun's heat a window lets into the house, from 0 to 1; lower keeps homes cooler, higher adds free winter heat.
entries.body: An SHGC of 0.25 means about a quarter of the solar heat hitting the window gets through. In hot climates a low SHGC cuts air conditioning; in cold climates a higher SHGC on sunny windows can provide useful heat. Low-e coatings can be chosen to raise or lower it.
entries.whyItMatters: Choosing the right SHGC for your climate and window orientation affects comfort and both heating and cooling bills, and it's part of the ENERGY STAR window criteria.

entries.caNote: NRCan's Energy Rating (ER) combines U-factor and solar gain into one number suited to Canadian heating climates.

entries.short: A Canadian window score that balances heat loss against free solar heat; higher is better, and ENERGY STAR Canada accepts ER 34 or more.
entries.body: The ER is a unitless number based on a window's U-factor and its solar heat gain (SHGC) under typical Canadian heating conditions. Because it credits solar gain, two windows with the same U-factor can have different ERs. It's most useful for comparing windows in heating-dominated climates.
entries.whyItMatters: ER is one of two ways a window can qualify for ENERGY STAR Canada, and rebates such as Ontario's HRSP require ENERGY STAR certified windows.

entries.short: Window glass with a thin, invisible metal coating that reflects heat, keeping more warmth in during winter and out in summer.
entries.body: The coating lets most visible light through but reflects heat back toward its source. Versions for cold climates keep solar gain high (see SHGC) to capture free heat, while solar-control versions keep it low to reduce cooling loads. Low-e is usually combined with double or triple glazing and an argon or krypton gas fill.
entries.whyItMatters: It's a main reason modern windows have much lower U-factors than old ones, and it reduces condensation on the inside pane in winter.

entries.short: A layer of insulation running unbroken over the framing, usually rigid boards on the outside of walls, to stop heat escaping through studs.
entries.body: Because studs and other framing conduct heat (see thermal bridging), insulation placed only between studs leaves gaps in protection. Continuous insulation, commonly rigid foam or other rigid boards, covers the framing too. It also keeps the wall sheathing warmer, which lowers condensation risk.
entries.whyItMatters: It's often the best way to raise wall performance during a re-siding job; ENERGY STAR recommends adding insulative sheathing when siding is replaced in most US climate zones.

entries.short: The continuous layer of materials in walls, ceilings and floors that stops air from leaking through the building envelope.
entries.body: An air barrier can be drywall sealed at the edges, sheathing with taped joints, house wrap, spray foam or polyethylene, as long as it's continuous and sealed at every joint and penetration. It's different from insulation, which slows heat but lets air pass, and from a vapour barrier, though one material can do both jobs.
entries.bodyUs: An air barrier can be drywall sealed at the edges, sheathing with taped joints, house wrap, spray foam or polyethylene, as long as it's continuous and sealed at every joint and penetration. It's different from insulation, which slows heat but lets air pass, and from a vapor barrier, though one material can do both jobs.
entries.whyItMatters: Without a continuous air barrier, insulation underperforms and moist indoor air leaks into walls and attics, causing condensation, mould and ice dams.

entries.short: A layer that slows water vapour moving through walls and ceilings, to keep it from condensing inside the structure.
entries.shortUs: A layer that slows water vapor moving through walls and ceilings, to keep it from condensing inside the structure.
entries.body: In cold climates, warm indoor air holds moisture that tries to diffuse outward through walls; a vapour barrier on the warm side, often polyethylene in Canada, slows it. Retarder is the more accurate term, because materials are rated by how much vapour they let through (perm rating), from almost none to quite a lot. Air leakage moves far more moisture than diffusion, so the air barrier matters even more.
entries.bodyUs: In cold climates, warm indoor air holds moisture that tries to diffuse outward through walls; a vapor barrier on the warm side, such as polyethylene sheeting or the kraft facing on batts, slows it. Retarder is the more accurate term, because materials are rated by how much vapor they let through (perm rating), from almost none to quite a lot. Air leakage moves far more moisture than diffusion, so the air barrier matters even more.
entries.whyItMatters: The wrong vapour control for your climate can trap moisture and rot walls, so auditors check it before recommending insulation, especially in basements.
entries.whyUs: The wrong vapor control for your climate can trap moisture and rot walls, so auditors check it before recommending insulation, especially in basements.

entries.short: The temperature at which air becomes saturated and water starts to condense on surfaces, like water beading on a cold glass.
entries.body: Air at a given humidity has a specific dew point, and any surface colder than that collects condensation. In winter, window glass, poorly insulated walls and sheathing behind badly detailed insulation can drop below the indoor air's dew point. Lowering indoor humidity or warming the surface prevents it.
entries.whyItMatters: Dew point explains where condensation, mould and rot will start, which shapes advice on insulation, vapour control and ventilation.
entries.whyUs: Dew point explains where condensation, mold and rot will start, which shapes advice on insulation, vapor control and ventilation.

entries.short: How much moisture the air holds compared with the most it could hold at that temperature, shown as a percentage.
entries.body: Warm air can hold more moisture than cold air, so the same amount of water vapour gives a lower RH once air is heated. An inexpensive hygrometer measures it. Too high encourages mould, dust mites and condensation; too low can feel uncomfortably dry.
entries.bodyUs: Warm air can hold more moisture than cold air, so the same amount of water vapor gives a lower RH once air is heated. An inexpensive hygrometer measures it. Too high encourages mold, dust mites and condensation; too low can feel uncomfortably dry.
entries.whyItMatters: High indoor humidity is a warning sign of poor ventilation or a moisture problem, and sealing a house tighter can raise it, so auditors check RH and may recommend an HRV, ERV or dehumidifier.

entries.short: Water that forms when humid air touches a surface colder than its dew point, on windows, cold pipes or hidden inside walls and attics.
entries.body: Condensation you can see, such as on windows, is a sign indoor humidity is high for the outdoor temperature. Hidden condensation inside walls, attics and rim joists happens when moist indoor air leaks or diffuses into the building envelope and meets cold surfaces. Over time it feeds mould and rot.

entries.whyItMatters: Auditors look for condensation stains and attic frost because they point to air leaks and humidity problems that need fixing before or along with insulation.

entries.short: The band of framing on top of the foundation wall around the edge of the floor; it's prone to air leaks and often poorly insulated.
entries.body: Called the header in Canada and the rim or band joist in the US, this strip runs around the basement ceiling where the floor framing meets the foundation. It has many joints, is often left uninsulated and is where the stack effect draws cold air in. Sealing the joints and insulating with rigid foam or spray foam is a common audit recommendation.
entries.whyItMatters: It's a small area with outsized air leakage, which is why audits so often flag it.
entries.caNote: NRCan notes that stuffing batts into the header doesn't stop air leaks; seal joints with caulking, and cover spray foam with a fire-resistant material if the basement ceiling doesn't cover it.
entries.bodyUs: Called the rim or band joist in the US (and the header in Canada), this strip runs around the basement ceiling where the floor framing meets the foundation. It has many joints, is often left uninsulated and is where the stack effect draws cold air in. Sealing the joints and insulating with rigid foam or spray foam is a common audit recommendation.

entries.short: A short wall, often in a 1½-storey house, that separates a finished upstairs room from the unheated attic space behind it.
entries.shortUs: A short wall, often in a 1½-story house, that separates a finished upstairs room from the unheated attic space behind it.
entries.body: Knee walls are often poorly insulated, and the floor joists beneath them are often open to the attic, letting cold air flow under the room above. NRCan's fix is to seal that opening flush with the back of the knee wall finish, then insulate and air seal the wall itself.
entries.whyItMatters: Rooms with knee walls are often hard to keep comfortable, so audits check them closely in older 1½-storey homes.
entries.whyUs: Rooms with knee walls are often hard to keep comfortable, so audits check them closely in older 1½-story homes.
entries.bodyUs: Knee walls are often poorly insulated, and the floor joists beneath them are often open to the attic, letting outside air flow under the room above. The usual fix is to seal that opening flush with the back of the knee wall finish, then insulate and air seal the wall itself.

entries.short: A hidden opening from the living space into the attic, around chimneys, plumbing stacks, wiring, pot lights or wall tops, that leaks warm air.
entries.body: Bypasses are often buried under insulation, so warm, moist air flows straight past it into the attic. Typical spots are the attic hatch, the tops of interior and exterior walls, plumbing stacks, chimneys (which need non-combustible fire-stop material), ducts, wiring holes and recessed lights. They're sealed from the attic before more insulation is added.
entries.whyItMatters: Sealing bypasses stops the biggest stack effect leaks, prevents attic frost and mould, and helps prevent ice dams.
entries.whyUs: Sealing bypasses stops the biggest stack effect leaks, prevents attic frost and mold, and helps prevent ice dams.
entries.caNote: NRCan notes standard recessed lights are hard to air seal and recommends approved airtight fixtures or covers.

entries.short: Soffit vents let outside air into the attic at the eaves, and baffles keep insulation from blocking that airflow.
entries.body: Most pitched attics are ventilated: air enters through vents in the soffit (the underside of the roof overhang) and leaves through roof or ridge vents. Baffles fixed between the rafters hold insulation back from the eaves so air can still flow, and insulation stops keep loose-fill from spilling into the soffits. NRCan advises against powered attic fans, which can pull house air into the attic.
entries.whyItMatters: Adding insulation without baffles can block ventilation and trap moisture in the attic, so audits check for them.

values.label: NRCan attic ventilation guidance
values.value: About 50% of vent openings at the soffits; total unobstructed vent area about 1:300 of insulated ceiling area (pitched roofs with accessible attics)

entries.bodyUs: Most pitched attics are ventilated: air enters through vents in the soffit (the underside of the roof overhang) and leaves through roof or ridge vents. Baffles fixed between the rafters hold insulation back from the eaves so air can still flow, and insulation stops keep loose-fill from spilling into the soffits. Powered attic fans are usually a poor idea, because they can pull conditioned house air into the attic through ceiling leaks.

entries.short: A ridge of ice at the roof edge that traps melting snow behind it, which can back up under shingles and leak into the house.
entries.body: Heat escaping into the attic warms the roof and melts the snow above; the water runs down to the cold overhang and refreezes. As the ice builds, water pools behind it and can work under the shingles. Ice dams usually form when there's a lot of snow on the roof.
entries.whyItMatters: Ice dams are usually a symptom of attic air leaks and thin insulation, so the lasting fix is to seal attic bypasses and insulate, not just remove the ice.

entries.short: Loose fibres of cellulose, fibreglass or mineral wool blown into attics or wall cavities by machine; fast, and good at filling around obstacles.
entries.shortUs: Loose fibers of cellulose, fiberglass or mineral wool blown into attics or wall cavities by machine; fast, and good at filling around obstacles.
entries.body: Cellulose is made mostly from recycled paper treated with borates for fire and pest resistance; fibreglass and mineral wool loose-fill are spun glass or rock fibres. In attics it's spread in an even layer to the target R-value, and in closed walls it's blown densely through small holes (see dense-pack insulation). Air sealing should be done first, and baffles installed at the eaves.

entries.short: Liquid foam sprayed in place that expands to insulate and air seal in one step; closed-cell is denser and higher R, open-cell lighter.
entries.body: Open-cell foam (about 0.5 lb per cubic foot) is soft and airtight at normal thickness but lets vapour through. Closed-cell foam (about 2 lb per cubic foot) is rigid, gives roughly R-6 per inch, resists water and acts as a vapour retarder at about 2 inches. Both are combustible and normally need a fire-protective covering, and installation is a job for certified contractors.

NRCan notes that polyiso's insulating value can drop in cold temperatures, so it suggests using it as an interior layer unless the product is rated for the cold. Taped or sealed boards can also act as an air barrier and, depending on type and thickness, slow vapour.

entries.short: A pebbly, brownish or silvery loose-fill attic insulation that may contain asbestos from a Montana mine, so it shouldn't be disturbed.
entries.body: Vermiculite looks like small, light, accordion-shaped pebbles. Much of the vermiculite sold until 1990 came from a mine near Libby, Montana, whose ore was contaminated with asbestos, and it was often sold as Zonolite, including in Canada. Health agencies say to assume it contains asbestos, leave it undisturbed, keep people and storage out of the attic and hire trained professionals before any work there.
entries.whyItMatters: Finding vermiculite changes the plan: attic air sealing and insulation shouldn't go ahead until it's assessed and, if needed, removed by professionals.

entries.short: A small air gap behind siding or brick that lets rainwater that gets past the cladding drain away and lets the wall dry.
entries.body: No cladding is perfectly waterproof. A rainscreen leaves a gap, often made with vertical strapping or the air space behind brick veneer, between the siding and the water-resistant layer behind it, so water drains and air carries moisture away. The gap shouldn't be filled with insulation or blocked at the bottom.
entries.whyItMatters: When an audit recommends exterior insulation or new siding, building in a drainage gap protects the wall from moisture damage.

values.label: Brick veneer air space (NRCan)
values.value: Typically 25–50 mm (1–2 in.), part of the drainage plane; don't insulate it

entries.short: A shiny foil layer, usually in attics, that reflects the sun's radiant heat; it helps most in hot, sunny climates.
entries.body: A radiant barrier reflects radiant heat instead of absorbing it, but it doesn't slow conducted heat the way insulation does. It needs an air space next to its shiny side to work, and dust on that side reduces its effect.
entries.whyItMatters: It does little for heating bills, so in colder climates compare it against simply adding insulation, and check your rebate rules, since some programs exclude it.

entries.short: Loose-fill insulation, usually cellulose, blown tightly into closed wall cavities through small holes so it fills them, resists settling and slows air movement.
entries.body: An installer drills small holes, typically 15–50 mm (⅝–2 in.), into each cavity and fills it through a hose until it's packed firm. NRCan gives a typical dense-pack density for cellulose of about 56 kg/m³ (3.5 lb per cubic foot); too little leaves voids that settle, and too much can make walls bulge. It's a common way to insulate empty walls in older homes without opening them up.
entries.whyItMatters: Dense-packing can add insulation and cut air leakage in uninsulated walls, but knob-and-tube wiring and moisture problems have to be dealt with first.

entries.short: An inexpensive gauge, often combined with a thermometer, that shows a room's relative humidity so you can keep it in a healthy range.
entries.body: Mechanical and electronic models are sold wherever room thermometers are, and one per house is usually enough, kept away from heat sources and chimneys. CMHC explains how to check one's accuracy with salty water in a sealed bag: after 8 to 12 hours it should read about 75%.

entries.short: An electric system that moves heat instead of making it: out of the house in summer and into it in winter, using a refrigerant loop.
entries.body: A heat pump works like a refrigerator that can run in either direction: it collects heat from outdoor air, the ground or water and pumps it indoors, then reverses to provide air conditioning. Because it moves heat rather than burning fuel or using electric resistance, it can deliver two to three or more units of heat per unit of electricity (see COP). Types include air-source, cold-climate, ground-source, ductless mini-split and ducted systems.
entries.whyItMatters: Heat pumps are central to most rebate programs, and they deliver the biggest savings when the house is sealed and insulated first and the system is sized with a proper load calculation.

entries.body: An outdoor unit with a fan and compressor connects by refrigerant lines to an indoor coil in your ductwork or to wall-mounted heads (see ductless mini-split). Its efficiency and capacity drop as outdoor temperatures fall, and it runs short defrost cycles in cold, damp weather. Cold-climate models keep heating efficiently well below freezing.
entries.whyItMatters: Choosing the right model for your climate, sizing it with a load calculation and planning auxiliary heat decide how much it will actually save.

entries.short: A heat pump that exchanges heat with the ground through buried pipes or well water, giving steady efficiency even in deep cold.
entries.body: Pipes buried in trenches or drilled boreholes (closed loop), or well water (open loop), carry heat between the ground and a heat pump inside the house. Because ground temperature is fairly stable year-round, efficiency stays high in winter and no defrost cycles are needed. The ground loop adds significant up-front cost compared with an air-source system.

entries.short: An air-source heat pump with wall- or ceiling-mounted indoor heads connected by refrigerant lines, needing no ductwork.
entries.body: One outdoor unit can serve one indoor head (single-zone) or several (multi-zone). Each head heats and cools its own area, which makes zoning easy and avoids duct losses, but rooms without a head, such as closed-off bedrooms, may not get enough heat. They suit homes without ducts, such as those heated by baseboards or boilers.
entries.whyItMatters: Mini-splits let homes without ducts switch to heat pump heating and cooling, but heads must be placed and sized to match each area's heat loss.

entries.short: A heat pump that heats and cools through ductwork, like central air conditioning, either on its own or paired with a furnace.
entries.body: An outdoor unit pairs with an indoor coil on a furnace or with a dedicated air handler, and warm or cool air flows through your existing ducts. Duct condition matters: leaky or undersized ducts reduce comfort and efficiency, so a duct leakage test is worth doing first. Paired with a gas furnace, it becomes a dual-fuel (hybrid) system.
entries.whyItMatters: For homes with good ductwork it's often the most straightforward whole-house heat pump option, and the indoor and outdoor parts must be a certified match (see AHRI certificate) to deliver the rated efficiency.

entries.short: Heat delivered divided by electricity used at a given moment; a COP of 3 means three units of heat for each unit of electricity.
entries.body: Electric baseboards and furnaces turn electricity into heat one-for-one, so their COP is about 1. Heat pumps reach COPs of 2 to 5 in mild weather because they move heat instead of making it, but COP falls as the outdoor temperature drops. Seasonal ratings such as HSPF average this over a whole winter.
entries.whyItMatters: COP at cold temperatures, such as −15°C (5°F), shows how cheaply a heat pump will run in your coldest weather and helps find the economic balance point against gas or oil.

entries.body: HSPF2 replaced HSPF in 2023 when US test procedures changed, and DOE says the old and new numbers aren't directly comparable. Ratings also depend on the climate assumed: Region IV represents a US Midwest-type climate, while Region V is colder, closer to Ottawa. Dividing HSPF by 3.412 gives an approximate seasonal COP.
entries.whyItMatters: It's the main heating-efficiency number on heat pump spec sheets, rebate rules and AHRI certificates.

entries.short: The share of a furnace's or boiler's fuel that ends up as heat in your home over a year; a 95% furnace loses about 5% up the vent.
entries.body: AFUE counts losses up the chimney or vent but not heat lost from leaky or uninsulated ducts, which can be large. Mid-efficiency furnaces are about 80%, and condensing furnaces reach 90% or more; older furnaces with standing pilot lights score lower.
entries.whyItMatters: Knowing your furnace's AFUE lets the auditor estimate what a replacement or a heat pump would save, and AFUE minimums decide what can legally be installed.

entries.short: Heating with electric elements that turn electricity directly into heat, such as baseboards, electric furnaces and heat pump backup strips.
entries.body: Electric resistance heat is simple and nearly 100% efficient at the point of use, but each kilowatt-hour gives only one kilowatt-hour of heat (a COP of about 1). A heat pump can deliver the same heat with much less electricity. Resistance elements are often used as auxiliary heat in heat pump systems.
entries.whyItMatters: Homes heated by baseboards or electric furnaces often have the most to gain from air sealing, insulation and a heat pump.

entries.short: A unit of heat energy; BTU per hour (BTU/h) measures how fast a furnace, heat pump or air conditioner delivers heating or cooling.
entries.body: One BTU is the heat needed to warm one pound of water by 1°F. Fuel energy is counted in BTU (or therms and MMBtu), while equipment capacity is given in BTU/h, for example a 60,000 BTU/h furnace or a 24,000 BTU/h (2-ton) heat pump. The metric equivalents are joules for energy and watts or kilowatts for capacity.
entries.whyItMatters: Comparing your home's calculated heat loss in BTU/h (see load calculation) with the equipment's rated capacity shows whether a system is sized correctly.

entries.short: A unit of heating and cooling capacity: one ton equals 12,000 BTU per hour (3.5 kW), based on the cooling from melting a ton of ice in a day.
entries.body: The term is based on the cooling effect of melting a ton of ice over a day. Capacity changes with outdoor temperature, so a heat pump's rated tonnage isn't what it delivers in deep cold; check its capacity at your design temperature.
entries.whyItMatters: Rules of thumb like 'one ton per 500 square feet' tend to oversize equipment; a proper load calculation sets the right tonnage.

entries.short: An engineering calculation of how much heating and cooling a house needs, room by room, used to size equipment correctly.
entries.body: It uses your home's insulation levels, windows, air leakage, size, orientation and local design temperature to estimate peak heat loss and heat gain in BTU/h. In the US the standard method is ACCA Manual J, with Manual S for choosing equipment and Manual D for duct design. Audit data such as a blower door result make it more accurate.
entries.whyItMatters: Correct sizing avoids oversizing and short cycling and improves comfort, and redoing it after envelope upgrades shows how much smaller a system you may need.

entries.short: A calculation of how fast a home loses heat on the coldest days it's designed for, used to size heating equipment; in Canada it follows CSA F280.
entries.shortUs: A calculation of how fast a home loses heat on the coldest days it's designed for, used to size heating equipment correctly.
entries.body: It adds up heat flow through walls, roof, floors, windows and doors plus air leakage and ventilation at the local design temperature, giving the heating capacity the house needs in BTU/h or watts. CSA F280, titled Determining the Required Capacity of Residential Space Heating and Cooling Appliances, covers both heating and cooling loads; the current edition, F280-12, was reaffirmed in 2025.
entries.whyItMatters: Sizing a heat pump or furnace from a proper heat-loss calculation, rather than matching the old equipment, avoids oversizing and helps rebate-funded upgrades perform as promised.

entries.bodyUs: It adds up heat flow through walls, roof, floors, windows and doors plus air leakage and ventilation at the local design temperature, giving the heating capacity the house needs in BTU/h. In the US the usual method is ACCA Manual J, which also works out the cooling load.

entries.short: The cold (or hot) outdoor temperature a heating or cooling system is sized for; colder than most winter days, but not the record low.
entries.body: Designers don't size for the coldest day ever recorded; they use a published temperature that's exceeded only for a small share of the season, so the system isn't oversized the rest of the time. The value comes from climate tables for your location and feeds the load calculation or heat-loss calculation.
entries.whyItMatters: Comparing a heat pump's capacity at your design temperature with your home's heat loss shows whether it can carry the house alone or will need auxiliary heat.
entries.caNote: Canadian design temperatures for code purposes come from the National Building Code's climatic data for each location and are used with CSA F280.

entries.short: The outdoor temperature where something changes: below the thermal balance point a heat pump needs help; below the economic one, fuel is cheaper.
entries.body: The thermal balance point is where the heat pump's output exactly matches the home's heat loss; below it, auxiliary heat makes up the difference. The economic balance point is where a backup fuel such as natural gas becomes cheaper per unit of heat than the heat pump, which depends on electricity and fuel prices and the heat pump's COP. Dual-fuel systems use it as their switchover temperature.
entries.whyItMatters: A tighter, better-insulated house has a lower thermal balance point, so the heat pump carries more of the winter, one reason audits pair envelope work with heat pumps.

entries.short: A second heat source — electric elements or a furnace — that helps a heat pump in very cold weather or during defrost.
entries.body: When it's colder than the heat pump's balance point, or while the outdoor unit defrosts, auxiliary heat fills the gap. It can be electric resistance elements in the air handler or baseboards, which can run alongside the heat pump, or a furnace or boiler, which runs instead of it (see dual-fuel). 'Emergency heat' is a thermostat setting that runs only the backup.
entries.whyItMatters: Electric backup heat costs much more to run than the heat pump, so good sizing, controls and thermostat settings that avoid triggering it are key to real savings.

entries.short: A heat pump paired with a gas, propane or oil furnace or boiler; controls switch to the fuel when it's colder or cheaper to do so.
entries.body: The heat pump handles most of the year and the furnace takes over below a set outdoor temperature, usually the economic balance point. The two don't run at the same time. It can make sense where winters are very cold, gas is relatively cheap or the existing furnace is fairly new.
entries.whyItMatters: It can cut fuel use and emissions while keeping a fuel backup, but rebate eligibility for hybrid setups varies by program.
entries.caNote: FortisBC's offering under the Canada Greener Homes Affordability Program includes dual-fuel heating systems (announced June 2026). In Quebec the idea is called dual energy (biénergie): Hydro-Québec's Rate DT bills electricity at a lower price while it's at or above −12°C or −15°C, depending on the region, and the system switches to its fuel backup below that.
entries.usNote: DOE's May 2026 HEEHR changes let households keep an existing fossil-fuel system when they add a heat pump.

entries.short: A compressor that ramps its speed up and down to match the heating or cooling needed, instead of switching fully on and off.
entries.body: An inverter drive lets the compressor run slowly for long periods in mild weather and speed up when it's very cold or hot. This avoids short cycling, keeps temperatures steadier and helps cold-climate heat pumps keep capacity in deep cold. Two-stage units are a simpler middle ground.
entries.whyItMatters: NEEP's current cold-climate specification requires variable capacity, so it's a quick marker of a heat pump built for cold weather.

values.label: NEEP ccASHP v4.0

entries.short: When heating or cooling equipment turns on and off frequently in short bursts instead of running in steady, longer cycles.
entries.body: It's often caused by oversizing: the system reaches the thermostat setting quickly and shuts off. Each start-up wastes energy and wears parts, and comfort suffers. Multi-stage or variable-speed equipment reduces it.
entries.whyItMatters: Short cycling is a sign the system may be oversized for the house, which is worth checking before replacing equipment after envelope upgrades shrink the load.
entries.caNote: NRCan suggests replacing a short-cycling furnace with a high-efficiency two-stage, three-stage or fully modulating model.

entries.short: Installing heating or cooling equipment with much more capacity than the house needs, usually from rules of thumb, not a load calculation.
entries.body: An oversized system reaches the thermostat setting quickly and shuts off, leading to short cycling, uneven temperatures, extra wear and wasted standby power, and it costs more to buy. Homes that have been air sealed and insulated may need much smaller equipment than what they had.
entries.whyItMatters: A proper load calculation or heat-loss calculation, done after envelope upgrades, avoids paying for capacity you don't need.

entries.short: A 1-to-16 rating of how well a furnace or air-handler filter catches airborne particles; higher numbers trap smaller particles.
entries.body: MERV comes from a standard test with particles between 0.3 and 10 microns. EPA suggests at least MERV 13 when upgrading, or the highest rating your system's fan and filter slot can handle. Ask an HVAC technician which filter your system can take.
entries.whyItMatters: A better filter is a low-cost indoor air quality upgrade, especially during wildfire smoke, but it only cleans air while the system fan is running.

entries.short: A ventilation system that swaps stale indoor air for fresh outdoor air while transferring heat from the outgoing air to the incoming air.
entries.body: Two fans move equal amounts of air in and out through a heat-exchange core, so fresh air arrives pre-warmed in winter. It runs continuously or on a schedule at low speed, with high speed for showers or cooking. Filters and the core need regular cleaning, and airflows should be balanced by a trained installer.
entries.whyItMatters: As a house gets tighter from air sealing, an HRV keeps indoor air quality and humidity under control without throwing away most of the heat.

entries.short: Like an HRV, but its core also transfers some moisture between the outgoing and incoming air, which helps manage humidity.
entries.body: In winter an ERV keeps some indoor moisture from being exhausted, reducing dryness; in humid weather it keeps some outdoor moisture out. It recovers heat like an HRV. It isn't a dehumidifier and won't fix a wet basement.
entries.whyItMatters: Choosing between an HRV and an ERV depends on climate and household moisture, so the auditor or ventilation designer should recommend which suits your home.

entries.body: Portable units sit in a room, while whole-house units connect to ductwork. Set one to hold relative humidity in the recommended range. A dehumidifier treats the symptom; leaks, poor drainage or air leakage causing the moisture still need fixing.
entries.whyItMatters: Controlling basement humidity helps prevent mould and musty smells, and ENERGY STAR certified models remove moisture with less electricity.

entries.short: Outdoor air deliberately brought into a house to replace air removed by big exhaust fans, range hoods, dryers or fireplaces.
entries.body: In a tight house, a powerful range hood or other exhaust can't pull air out unless the same amount can get in. Without a planned path, replacement air may come down a chimney or flue, causing backdrafting, or the fan simply won't work well. Make-up air systems open a damper, sometimes with heating, when the exhaust runs.
entries.whyItMatters: Auditors look at exhaust capacity during a combustion safety test, and adding a big range hood after air sealing may call for make-up air.

entries.short: Dividing a home into areas with separate thermostats so each can be heated or cooled only when and as much as needed.
entries.body: Zoning can use motorized dampers in ducts, separate equipment for each floor, or ductless mini-split heads in individual rooms. It helps homes where some areas run hot or cold, such as upper floors that overheat while basements stay cool.
entries.whyItMatters: Zoning can improve comfort and trim energy use, but it doesn't fix the air leaks or insulation gaps that often cause hot and cold rooms in the first place.

entries.short: A Wi-Fi-connected thermostat that schedules, learns or adjusts temperatures automatically and can be controlled from your phone.
entries.body: Smart thermostats make setback easy and can show energy-use reports. With a heat pump, choose one designed for heat pumps so setbacks don't trigger expensive auxiliary heat.
entries.whyItMatters: It's an inexpensive upgrade that many programs rebate, and the savings depend on actually using setbacks.

Some slow-responding hot-water (hydronic) systems also gain little.

entries.short: The fluid a heat pump or air conditioner pumps around to move heat; newer systems use R-454B or R-32 instead of the older R-410A.
entries.body: The refrigerant absorbs heat as it evaporates in one coil and gives it off as it condenses in the other, which is how a heat pump moves heat. Many refrigerants are strong greenhouse gases, rated by their global warming potential (GWP), so US rules have moved new home systems from R-410A (GWP 2,088) to R-454B (465) and R-32 (675).
entries.whyItMatters: The refrigerant on a quote shows whether you're being offered current equipment or older R-410A stock, and some rebate programs accept only low-GWP models.

entries.short: A short, automatic cycle that melts frost off a heat pump's outdoor coil or an HRV's core in freezing weather; it's a normal part of winter operation.
entries.body: When it's near or below freezing, moisture in the air freezes on a heat pump's outdoor coil, so the unit briefly switches to cooling mode, with the outdoor fan off, to send hot refrigerant through the coil and melt the frost. Supplementary heat may run meanwhile so the house doesn't get cool air. Most HRVs have an automatic defrost mode too, which starts when incoming air is colder than about −5°C (23°F) and clears frost from the core.
entries.whyItMatters: Defrost uses energy and lowers winter efficiency, which is one reason seasonal and cold-weather ratings matter more than mild-weather numbers, and repeated freezing can signal a fault.

entries.short: A furnace, boiler or water heater that takes combustion air from the room and relies on hot exhaust rising up a chimney, so house pressure can reverse it.
entries.body: These appliances, including many older furnaces and standard gas water heaters, have an opening called a draft hood and depend on the chimney's natural draft to carry exhaust away. If exhaust fans, a dryer or a fireplace depressurize the house, or the chimney is cold or blocked, exhaust can spill back indoors. CMHC warns against pairing a natural-draft furnace with a powerful kitchen exhaust fan.
entries.whyItMatters: Natural-draft appliances are the ones most likely to backdraft, so auditors test them before and after air sealing and may suggest a sealed-combustion replacement.

entries.bodyUs: These appliances, including many older furnaces and standard gas water heaters, have an opening called a draft hood and depend on the chimney's natural draft to carry exhaust away. If exhaust fans, a dryer or a fireplace depressurize the house, or the chimney is cold or blocked, exhaust can spill back indoors. Pairing one with a powerful kitchen exhaust fan without make-up air is a classic cause of backdrafting.

entries.short: A furnace, boiler, water heater or fireplace that brings in combustion air from outdoors through its own pipe and vents exhaust straight outside.
entries.body: Because the burner is sealed off from indoor air, house pressure from exhaust fans or a tight building envelope can't pull exhaust back inside the way it can with a natural-draft appliance. Many condensing furnaces, newer water heaters and gas fireplaces are built this way. Fan-assisted appliances that still draw air from the room sit in between: CMHC says they're often resistant to spillage, while sealed combustion restricts it further.
entries.whyItMatters: NRCan calls switching spillage-prone equipment to direct-vent or sealed-combustion models the first line of defence against combustion gases, which makes deeper air sealing safer.
entries.whyUs: Switching spillage-prone equipment to direct-vent or sealed-combustion models is the surest defense against combustion gases, which makes deeper air sealing safer.
entries.bodyUs: Because the burner is sealed off from indoor air, house pressure from exhaust fans or a tight building envelope can't pull exhaust back inside the way it can with a natural-draft appliance. Many condensing furnaces, newer water heaters and gas fireplaces are built this way. Fan-assisted appliances that still draw air from the room sit in between: they resist spillage better than natural-draft ones, and sealed combustion restricts it further.

entries.short: A non-condensing gas or oil furnace, around 80% efficient, that sends its exhaust up a chimney; most new gas furnaces sold in Canada must now be condensing.
entries.body: Mid-efficiency furnaces were the standard upgrade before condensing models: they don't recover the heat in their exhaust's water vapour, so roughly a fifth of the fuel's energy goes up the flue. Since July 3, 2019 most new gas furnaces sold in Canada must reach 95% AFUE, which only condensing furnaces do, while the US minimum is still 80%. NRCan notes that after major air sealing a mid-efficiency furnace runs less often, so its chimney can get colder between firings and draft poorly.
entries.bodyUs: Mid-efficiency furnaces were the standard upgrade before condensing models: they don't recover the heat in their exhaust's water vapor, so roughly a fifth of the fuel's energy goes up the flue. The federal minimum for most new gas furnaces in the US is still 80% AFUE, so they're still sold alongside condensing models rated 90% or more. After major air sealing a mid-efficiency furnace runs less often, so its chimney can get colder between firings and draft poorly.
entries.whyItMatters: If your mid-efficiency furnace is nearing replacement, an audit helps you compare a condensing furnace, a heat pump or a dual-fuel system for your home.

entries.short: The US industry standard for calculating how much heating and cooling a house needs, room by room, so equipment can be sized correctly.
entries.body: Manual J is published by the Air Conditioning Contractors of America (ACCA); the current version is the 8th edition (ANSI/ACCA 2 Manual J – 2016). It uses the home's dimensions, insulation, windows, air leakage, ducts and local design conditions to estimate peak heat loss and heat gain. ACCA says national building codes and most state and local jurisdictions require a load calculation done to Manual J.
entries.whyItMatters: Ask for the Manual J report with any heating or cooling quote: it's the evidence that the size wasn't picked by rule of thumb.

entries.short: The US industry standard for choosing heating and cooling equipment whose real capacity, from the maker's data, fits the home's calculated loads.
entries.body: Manual S takes the heating and cooling loads from Manual J and the manufacturer's performance data, then checks that a candidate system falls within size limits that account for the local climate. The 3rd edition (ANSI/ACCA 3 Manual S – 2023) expanded the size tolerances for variable-capacity heat pumps. It covers heating, cooling, dehumidifying and humidifying equipment.
entries.whyItMatters: It's the step that stops a too-big or too-small unit from being installed even after a proper load calculation.

entries.short: The US industry standard for designing and sizing a home's ducts so each room gets the airflow the heating and cooling equipment is meant to deliver.
entries.body: Manual D starts from the airflow each room needs and the blower's performance, then sizes the supply and return ducts to deliver it. It's ACCA's ANSI-recognized duct design method, now in its third edition. Ducts that are too small or poorly laid out can leave rooms hot or cold even when the equipment is the right size.
entries.whyItMatters: When a heat pump replaces a furnace, the existing ducts may not carry enough air, and a Manual D check shows what needs to change.

entries.short: A widely used list of cold-climate air-source heat pumps, kept by Northeast Energy Efficiency Partnerships, with tested performance down to 5°F (−15°C).
entries.body: Northeast Energy Efficiency Partnerships (NEEP) publishes the Cold Climate Air Source Heat Pump Specification and a product list of models that meet it; version 4.0 has applied since January 1, 2023. Listings give capacity and efficiency at low outdoor temperatures, which contractors use for sizing, and some rebate programs require a listed model. A version 5.0 proposed in July 2026 would rely on ENERGY STAR Cold Climate certification instead, but NEEP still shows it as coming, with no effective date.
entries.whyItMatters: If a rebate requires a NEEP-listed or cold-climate model, check the exact indoor and outdoor pairing on the list before you sign.

entries.short: A heat pump's average heat output per unit of electricity over a whole heating season, including defrost and backup heat, instead of at one temperature.
entries.body: A single COP describes one moment, such as 3.0 at 8°C (46°F), but efficiency falls as it gets colder and drops further when backup heat runs. Seasonal COP averages all of that over a location's winter, so it's the number that drives your heating bill. Dividing a heat pump's HSPF2 by 3.412 gives a rough seasonal COP for the rating's test climate.
entries.whyItMatters: Energy cost calculators use seasonal COP to compare a heat pump with gas, oil or baseboards, so a realistic value for your climate matters more than the best-case rating.

values.label: From HSPF2
values.value: Seasonal COP ≈ HSPF2 ÷ 3.412 (for example, HSPF2 8.5 ≈ 2.5)

values.label: Electric baseboards and furnaces
values.value: 1.0: one unit of heat for each unit of electricity

entries.term: Region IV and Region V (HSPF test climates)
entries.short: The two climates heat pump heating ratings are usually given for: Region IV, like the US Midwest, and the colder Region V, closer to southern Canada.
entries.body: HSPF and HSPF2 depend on the winter assumed in the rating calculation, so the same heat pump scores lower for Region V than for Region IV. US spec sheets and the AHRI directory usually show Region IV, while NRCan says Region V covers most of the southern half of the provinces and best reflects performance around Ottawa. Real seasonal efficiency is lower still where winters have more heating degree-days.
entries.whyItMatters: Compare heat pumps using the same region's rating, and in most of Canada look for the Region V figure.

values.value: Region 4 represents climates like the US Midwest; Region 5 covers most of the southern half of the provinces and best reflects the Ottawa area

entries.shortUs: The two climates heat pump heating ratings are usually given for: Region IV, like the Midwest, and the colder Region V, like the northern tier of states.
entries.bodyUs: HSPF and HSPF2 depend on the winter assumed in the rating calculation, so the same heat pump scores lower for Region V than for Region IV. Spec sheets and the AHRI directory usually show Region IV. Real seasonal efficiency is lower still where winters have more heating degree days.
entries.whyUs: Compare heat pumps using the same region's rating, and in the coldest northern states look for the Region V figure.

entries.short: A high-efficiency, variable-speed fan motor for furnaces, air handlers and HRVs that uses far less electricity than older motors, especially at low speed.
entries.body: Older furnaces use permanent split capacitor (PSC) motors, which run at about 60%–65% efficiency at full speed and less when slowed down. An electronically commutated motor (ECM, also called a brushless DC motor) stays near 80% efficient even at reduced speed, so the furnace fan can circulate ventilation air or filter smoke cheaply. NRCan says a brushless DC motor can cut average furnace electricity use by more than 70% when the fan runs continuously.
entries.whyItMatters: If you run the furnace fan to spread HRV air or filter wildfire smoke, an ECM motor keeps that from adding a big electricity cost.

values.label: Motor efficiency (NRCan)
values.value: PSC motors 60%–65% at peak; ECM motors near 80% even at reduced speed

values.label: Continuous circulation (NRCan)
values.value: More than 70% less furnace electricity with a brushless DC motor

entries.bodyUs: Older furnaces use permanent split capacitor (PSC) motors, which run at about 60%–65% efficiency at full speed and less when slowed down. An electronically commutated motor (ECM, also called a brushless DC motor) stays near 80% efficient even at reduced speed, so the furnace fan can circulate ventilation air or filter smoke cheaply, and it uses far less electricity when the fan runs continuously.

entries.short: How many output levels heating or cooling equipment has: single-stage runs fully on or off, two-stage adds a low setting, and variable-speed adjusts smoothly.
entries.body: Single-stage heat pumps and furnaces always run at full output, which is simple but leads to more on-off cycling. Two-stage and multi-stage models run on low most of the time and switch to high in extreme weather, while variable-speed (inverter) and fully modulating models adjust continuously. NRCan notes that heat pumps at the minimum efficiency ratings are typically single-speed.
entries.whyItMatters: More stages usually mean steadier temperatures and less short cycling, which matters most once air sealing has shrunk the home's heating and cooling needs.

entries.term: Certified wood stove (EPA or CSA B415.1)
entries.short: A wood stove or insert tested to meet smoke emission limits under the US EPA standard or Canada's CSA B415.1; it burns cleaner and more efficiently.
entries.body: Since 2020, new wood heaters sold in the US must emit no more than 2.0 grams of particles an hour when tested with crib wood, or 2.5 grams with cord wood. CSA B415.1 is the Canadian test of heat output, efficiency and emissions, and some rebates require one standard or the other. CMHC's wood-heating guide says certified, clean-burning appliances cut smoke by as much as 90% compared with conventional ones.
entries.whyItMatters: Certification is the first thing to check on a wood stove: older uncertified models smoke more and burn more wood for the same heat.

values.value: 2.0 g/h with crib wood or 2.5 g/h with cord wood, down from 4.5 g/h under the 2015 limits

values.label: Effect (CMHC wood-heating guide)
values.value: Certified appliances cut smoke by as much as 90%; advanced stoves are about one-third more efficient on average

entries.bodyUs: Since 2020, new wood heaters sold in the US must emit no more than 2.0 grams of particles an hour when tested with crib wood, or 2.5 grams with cord wood. Certified models carry a metal EPA label, and some rebates require certification.

entries.short: Short for heating, ventilation and air conditioning: the equipment and ducts that heat, cool and move fresh air through a home.
entries.body: An HVAC system can include a furnace or boiler, a heat pump or air conditioner, ductwork, an HRV or ERV, and the thermostat and controls. HVAC contractors install and service this equipment, while an energy auditor tests how well it works with the rest of the house.
entries.whyItMatters: Audits often recommend fixing the building envelope before replacing HVAC equipment, because a tighter, better-insulated house needs a smaller system.

entries.short: An electric water heater with a small heat pump on top that pulls heat from the surrounding air, using far less electricity than a standard tank.
entries.body: The heat pump does most of the work, with electric elements as backup for heavy demand. It cools and dehumidifies the room it sits in, which can help in a damp basement in summer. It needs enough space, airflow and a condensate drain, and 120-volt plug-in models make replacing a standard tank easier.
entries.whyItMatters: Water heating is a big slice of home energy use, and a heat pump water heater uses a third to a half of the electricity of a standard electric tank, so it's often a high-value upgrade that many programs rebate.

entries.short: A water heater with no storage tank that heats water only as it flows, avoiding the heat a tank loses while it sits waiting.
entries.body: A tankless unit fires up when a hot tap opens, so it avoids the standby losses of keeping a tank hot. Its flow capacity is limited, so households that run several hot taps at once may need a larger unit. Gas models need proper venting and gas supply.
entries.whyItMatters: Savings are largest for households using moderate amounts of hot water; for all-electric homes a heat pump water heater usually saves more.

entries.short: A water heater's overall efficiency rating from a standard daily hot-water test; higher is better, and the best heat pump models score above 3.
entries.body: UEF compares water heaters of the same type and draw pattern (how much hot water a household uses). Gas storage tanks score below 1, efficient gas tankless and condensing units approach 1, standard electric tanks are just under 1, and heat pump water heaters reach 3 to nearly 4. Older literature uses the energy factor (EF), which isn't directly comparable.
entries.whyItMatters: Comparing UEF lets you estimate operating costs between options and check rebate eligibility.

entries.short: A copper section of the main drain that uses warm shower water going down the drain to preheat the cold water coming in.
entries.body: Cold water is routed through coils wrapped around a vertical drain stack, and heat passes through the copper while the two streams never mix. It has no moving parts and works best when warm water is going down the drain while fresh water is drawn at the same time, mostly during showers.
entries.whyItMatters: It's an easy add-on during plumbing renovations or new construction and trims water-heating energy for the life of the house.
entries.caNote: NRCan keeps a searchable list of tested drain-water heat recovery units.

entries.short: The unit on your electricity bill: one kilowatt-hour is 1,000 watts used for one hour, such as a 100-watt bulb left on for 10 hours.
entries.body: A kilowatt (kW) is a rate of power, while a kilowatt-hour is energy used over time. Your meter counts kWh and the bill multiplies them by the price per kWh, which may vary by time of day (see time-of-use pricing). Comparing kWh with gas use in therms, cubic metres or gigajoules requires a conversion.

Your meter counts kWh and the bill multiplies them by the price per kWh, which may vary by time of day (see time-of-use pricing). Comparing kWh with gas use in therms, cubic meters or gigajoules requires a conversion.
entries.whyItMatters: Twelve months of kWh readings show your baseload and how much electricity goes to heating or cooling, which helps the auditor estimate savings.

entries.body: Utilities convert the gas volume your meter records, often in hundreds of cubic feet (CCF), into therms using the gas's heat content. A dekatherm is 10 therms. To compare with electricity, 1 therm is about 29.3 kWh.
entries.whyItMatters: Your yearly therms for heating, compared with heating degree days, let an auditor estimate how much air sealing, insulation or new equipment would save.

entries.body: One gigajoule is a billion joules, and a megajoule (MJ) is one-thousandth of a gigajoule. Some Canadian utilities bill natural gas by the GJ and others by cubic metres (m³), and the EnerGuide rating expresses a home's yearly energy use in GJ so different fuels can be added together.
entries.whyItMatters: Your EnerGuide rating and projected savings are reported in GJ, so knowing the conversions lets you translate them into dollars on your bills.

entries.body: Your meter measures gas volume, and the bill may show cubic metres, gigajoules or both, adjusted for the gas's heat content. One cubic metre is about 35.3 cubic feet. Annual gas use in m³, compared with heating degree days, shows how efficiently your house is heated.
entries.whyItMatters: Auditors use your m³ history to check the energy model and estimate savings from upgrades or from switching to a heat pump.
