entries.short: Electricity prices that change with the time of day, usually cheapest overnight and highest when demand peaks.
entries.body: With TOU pricing the same kWh costs more at peak times and less off-peak, so shifting flexible loads such as laundry, dishwashing, EV charging and water heating saves money. Heat pumps and smart thermostats can be scheduled with prices in mind, though comfort comes first.
entries.whyItMatters: Your rate plan changes the dollar value of savings and can tilt the economics of heat pumps, batteries and water-heater timers.
entries.caNote: In Ontario the Ontario Energy Board sets three regulated price plans each November 1: time-of-use (on-, mid- and off-peak prices), ultra-low overnight, and tiered. Check oeb.ca for this year's prices.
entries.usNote: DOE notes many utilities offer off-peak programs or time-based rates; availability depends on your utility and state.

entries.short: The energy a home uses no matter the season — fridge, lights, electronics, water heating and standby power — apart from heating and cooling.
entries.body: Auditors estimate baseload from your lowest-use months, when neither heating nor cooling is running much. Use above that line in winter is roughly heating, and above it in summer is cooling. Devices drawing power while switched 'off' add to it.
entries.whyItMatters: Separating baseload from heating and cooling shows which upgrades matter most; a high baseload points to appliances, water heating or standby use rather than the building envelope.

values.label: Standby power (DOE)
values.value: Electronics drawing power while off can add 5%–10% to a monthly utility bill

entries.short: A measure of how cold a place or period is: the sum of how far each day's average temperature falls below a base of 18°C or 65°F.
entries.body: A day averaging 8°C counts 10 heating degree days on the 18°C base, and a day at or above the base counts zero. Monthly or yearly totals track heating demand, which is why climate zones and utility bill analysis use them. Canadian figures use °C (base 18°C) and US figures use °F (base 65°F), so US totals are about 1.8 times larger.
entries.whyItMatters: Dividing heating energy use by HDD lets an auditor compare winters fairly and measure the real effect of upgrades.

values.value: 18°C in Canada (ECCC); 65°F in the US (EIA)

entries.shortCa: A measure of how cold a place is: each day adds how far its average temperature falls below 18°C. More degree-days means more heating.
entries.shortUs: A measure of how cold a place is: each day adds how far its average temperature falls below 65°F. More degree days means more heating.
entries.bodyCa: A day averaging 8°C adds 10 heating degree-days; a day at or above 18°C adds none. Yearly totals track how much heating a house needs, which is why building codes, climate zones and bill analysis use them. Canadian totals use °C, so they look smaller than US figures for the same climate (multiply by 1.8 to compare).
entries.bodyUs: A day averaging 50°F adds 15 heating degree days; a day at or above 65°F adds none. Yearly totals track how much heating a house needs, which is why climate zones and bill analysis use them. US totals use °F; Canadian figures use °C and look smaller (multiply them by 1.8 to compare).

entries.short: A measure of how hot a place or period is: the sum of how far each day's average temperature rises above a base of 18°C or 65°F.
entries.body: A day averaging 78°F counts 13 cooling degree days on the 65°F base. Totals track air-conditioning demand, and places with many more CDD than HDD are cooling-dominated.
entries.whyItMatters: CDD help an auditor judge how much cooling efficiency (SEER2, EER2), window SHGC and attic radiant barriers matter in your climate.

entries.shortCa: A measure of how hot a place is: each day adds how far its average temperature rises above 18°C. More degree-days means more cooling.
entries.shortUs: A measure of how hot a place is: each day adds how far its average temperature rises above 65°F. More degree days means more air conditioning.
entries.bodyCa: A day averaging 24°C adds 6 cooling degree-days. Yearly totals track air-conditioning demand. Every Canadian city has far more heating than cooling degree-days, but hot-summer places still need cooling planned in, especially when a heat pump replaces a furnace.
entries.bodyUs: A day averaging 78°F adds 13 cooling degree days. Yearly totals track air-conditioning demand. Where cooling degree days outnumber heating degree days, as in Phoenix, Houston or Miami, the climate is cooling-dominated and summer bills matter most.

entries.short: Yearly energy use divided by floor area, such as kBtu per square foot or GJ per square metre, for comparing homes of different sizes.
entries.shortUs: Yearly energy use divided by floor area, such as kBtu per square foot, for comparing homes of different sizes.
entries.body: Total energy use makes small homes look good and big ones look bad; EUI levels the field. It can be calculated from your bills or from an energy model. Comparing EUI before and after upgrades, or against similar homes, shows how efficient the house really is.
entries.whyItMatters: EUI is a simple way to benchmark your home and track progress toward targets such as net-zero ready.

entries.short: Canada's official home energy rating: a home's estimated yearly energy use in gigajoules (GJ/year), where lower is better.
entries.body: A registered energy advisor inspects the home, runs a blower door test and builds a HOT2000 model to estimate the net energy it uses in a year. The label shows that rating, energy use by fuel and end use, greenhouse gas emissions, and a comparison with a reference house — the same home built to typical new-home requirements. You also get a Homeowner Information Sheet and a Renovation Upgrade Report.
entries.whyItMatters: Programs that use evaluations check upgrades against pre- and post-retrofit EnerGuide ratings, and the label is a credible way to show a home's efficiency when buying or selling.

entries.short: A US home energy score where 100 equals a typical home built to 2006 standards and 0 is net zero; each point is about 1% of energy use.
entries.body: A certified RESNET HERS rater inspects and tests the home, including blower door and duct leakage tests, and models it against a reference home of the same size and shape. A score of 70 means about 30% more efficient than that reference, and 130 about 30% less efficient. It's used mostly for new homes and code compliance.
entries.whyItMatters: HERS scores appear in new-home marketing and in ENERGY STAR and DOE new-home programs, so they let buyers compare efficiency.

entries.short: A US Department of Energy 1-to-10 rating of an existing home's expected energy use, a bit like a miles-per-gallon rating for houses.
entries.body: A trained assessor records the home's envelope, heating, cooling and hot water systems, and DOE's model estimates its energy use, normalized for local weather so scores compare across climates. A 10 ranks among the most efficient homes and 5 is about average.
entries.whyItMatters: It gives buyers and owners a simple, comparable number for an existing home.

entries.short: The government-backed blue label for products and some homes that beat minimum efficiency standards by meeting stricter criteria.
entries.body: ENERGY STAR sets specifications for products such as heat pumps, windows, water heaters, dehumidifiers and appliances, and certified models are tested and listed. The US program is moving from EPA to the Department of Energy, and Canada runs ENERGY STAR Canada under an agreement with the US. Many rebates require ENERGY STAR certification.
entries.whyItMatters: Checking for ENERGY STAR (or ENERGY STAR Most Efficient) is a quick way to shortlist efficient equipment and confirm rebate eligibility.

entries.short: A yearly ENERGY STAR designation for the top-performing certified products in a category, a step above regular ENERGY STAR.
entries.body: Each year ENERGY STAR publishes stricter criteria for selected categories such as heat pumps, windows, dehumidifiers and appliances, and products that meet them carry the Most Efficient mark for that year. It's a shortcut to the best available efficiency, though price and fit for your home still matter.
entries.whyItMatters: Some programs have required it, including the US window tax credit that ended after 2025, so check your program's rules.

values.label: Latest designation confirmed
values.value: 2025 — NRCan lists 13 categories, including air-source and ground-source heat pumps, windows and sliding glass doors, and dehumidifiers; a 2026 designation could not be confirmed

entries.whyCa: Some rebate programs require it for certain products, so check your program's rules before you buy.

entries.short: Proof that a specific indoor and outdoor heat pump or air conditioner combination was tested and certified, with its official ratings.
entries.body: Heat pumps and air conditioners are rated as matched systems: a particular outdoor unit with a particular indoor coil or air handler. The free AHRI Directory of Certified Product Performance, from the Air-Conditioning, Heating, and Refrigeration Institute, lists each certified combination with a reference number and its efficiency ratings, such as SEER2, EER2 and HSPF2, and capacity. Ask your contractor for the AHRI certificate for the exact models quoted.
entries.whyItMatters: Many utility rebates require the AHRI reference number, and a mismatched indoor unit can mean lower efficiency, discomfort and early failure.
entries.caNote: Canadian rebate programs may also ask for the AHRI reference number of the installed system; check your program's terms.

entries.short: Efficiency levels set by the Consortium for Energy Efficiency that utilities and programs use to decide which equipment qualifies.
entries.body: CEE, a consortium of energy efficiency program administrators, publishes tiered specifications for products such as heat pumps, furnaces and water heaters, with higher tiers meaning higher efficiency. Programs pick a tier as their bar, and tiers are updated over time, so equipment that qualified one year may not the next.
entries.whyItMatters: Rebate rules often reference a CEE tier, and from 2023 to 2025 the US 25C tax credit did too.

values.label: 25C tax credit rule, 2023–2025 (IRS)
values.value: Heat pumps, central air conditioners, water heaters, furnaces and boilers had to meet the highest CEE tier, excluding any advanced tier, in effect at the start of the year

values.label: NEEP v5.0 proposal (July 2026)
values.value: CEE Tier 1 Path A would be one route to cold-climate listing

entries.short: A net-zero home produces as much energy as it uses in a year, usually with solar; a net-zero ready home is built so it could, once panels go on.
entries.body: These homes start with a very efficient building envelope and equipment, then add on-site renewable energy to cover what's left. Ready homes meet the efficiency requirements without the renewables yet. Existing homes can get there through deep energy retrofits.
entries.whyItMatters: Net-zero labels give a clear target for deep retrofits and new builds, and an audit shows how far your home is from it.

values.label: HERS Index equivalent (RESNET)
values.value: A score of 0 means the home produces as much energy as it uses

values.label: CHBA Net Zero Home Labelling Program
values.value: Net Zero and Net Zero Ready labels for new homes and renovations; 45 labelled renovations reported

values.label: DOE Efficient New Homes (formerly Zero Energy Ready Home)
values.value: Certified homes acquired before July 1, 2026 could qualify for the 45L builder credit of up to $5,000

entries.caNote: The Canadian Home Builders' Association runs Net Zero and Net Zero Ready labels for both new homes and renovations.
entries.usNote: DOE renamed its Zero Energy Ready Home program 'DOE Efficient New Homes'; the related 45L builder tax credit ends for homes acquired after June 30, 2026.

entries.short: How many years an upgrade takes to pay for itself: the cost after rebates divided by the yearly savings.
entries.body: If air sealing costs $1,200 after rebates and saves $300 a year, the simple payback is four years. It's easy to understand but ignores what happens after payback, changing energy prices, maintenance, financing costs and benefits such as comfort and health.
entries.whyItMatters: Audit reports often rank upgrades by payback, so understanding its limits helps you weigh quick wins against longer-lived investments.

values.label: Formula
values.value: Payback (years) = net cost ÷ annual savings

values.label: Worked example
values.value: $1,200 of air sealing after rebates that saves $300 a year pays back in 4 years

entries.short: The yearly savings from an upgrade as a percentage of its cost; a 4-year payback is roughly a 25% annual return.
entries.body: Simple ROI is annual savings divided by net cost, the flip side of simple payback. It lets you compare an efficiency upgrade with other uses of money, but a fair comparison also accounts for the upgrade's lifespan and upkeep (see lifecycle cost).
entries.whyItMatters: Seeing upgrades as investments makes it clearer when financing such as on-bill or PACE can still leave you ahead.

values.label: Formula
values.value: ROI = annual savings ÷ net cost × 100%

values.label: Example
values.value: $300 a year saved on a $1,200 project = 25% a year

entries.short: The total cost of owning an option over its life — purchase, installation, energy, maintenance and replacement — minus rebates.
entries.body: Comparing lifecycle costs shows when a pricier but more efficient system costs less over its working life. Analysts often discount future costs and savings to today's dollars.
entries.whyItMatters: It's the fairest way to compare a heat pump with a furnace, or a heat pump water heater with a standard tank.

entries.short: The number of hours a heating or cooling system would have to run flat out to deliver a whole season's heating or cooling.
entries.body: Real equipment cycles on and off and often runs below full output, so energy calculators turn a season's demand into an equivalent number of hours at full capacity. NRCan's air conditioner cost formula does this with cooling degree-days: 24 × cooling degree-days ÷ (summer design temperature − 18°C). Multiply the full-load hours by the unit's capacity and divide by its efficiency to estimate the energy it uses.
entries.whyItMatters: It's how a calculator turns your local climate into a yearly kWh estimate for an air conditioner or heat pump: the more full-load hours, the more a high-efficiency unit saves.

values.label: NRCan cooling formula (base 18°C)
values.value: Full-load hours = 24 × cooling degree-days ÷ (summer outdoor design temperature − 18)

values.label: Worked example
values.value: 200 cooling degree-days and a 30°C design temperature: 24 × 200 ÷ 12 = 400 full-load hours

values.label: Cooling formula (base 65°F)
values.value: Full-load hours = 24 × cooling degree days ÷ (summer outdoor design temperature − 65)

values.label: Worked example
values.value: 1,000 cooling degree days and a 95°F design temperature: 24 × 1,000 ÷ 30 = 800 full-load hours

entries.bodyUs: Real equipment cycles on and off and often runs below full output, so energy calculators turn a season's demand into an equivalent number of hours at full capacity. A common method uses cooling degree days: 24 × cooling degree days ÷ (summer design temperature − 65°F). Multiply the full-load hours by the unit's capacity and divide by its efficiency to estimate the energy it uses.

entries.short: The Canadian label on appliances and some heating, cooling and ventilation equipment that shows a model's energy use or efficiency next to similar models.
entries.body: EnerGuide is the Government of Canada's official mark for rating the energy use or efficiency of household appliances, heating and ventilation equipment, air conditioners, houses and vehicles. For products covered by federal rules, the label places the model on a scale against similar models; on a room air conditioner, for example, it gives the CEER efficiency rating, where higher is better. ENERGY STAR models may show the ENERGY STAR symbol on the same label.
entries.whyItMatters: Comparing EnerGuide labels in the store is a quick way to estimate running costs, and it's a different thing from the EnerGuide rating for your home.

values.label: Room air conditioners (NRCan)
values.value: The label is mandatory and shows the CEER rating, cooling capacity in Btu/h and the range for similar models

entries.term: kBtu and MMBtu (thousand and million BTU)
entries.short: Shorthand for large amounts of heat energy: kBtu is a thousand BTU and MMBtu is a million BTU, used to compare fuels and yearly energy use.
entries.body: Fuel prices and home energy use are often stated per million BTU so gas, oil, propane and electricity can be compared on the same basis. One MMBtu equals 10 therms, or about 293 kWh. On equipment, MBH means thousands of BTU per hour.
entries.whyItMatters: Cost per million BTU of delivered heat is the fairest way to compare a heat pump with a furnace or boiler, once each system's efficiency is counted.

values.label: Conversions
values.value: 1 kBtu = 1,000 BTU; 1 MMBtu = 1,000,000 BTU = 10 therms ≈ 293 kWh
values.source: Arithmetic from EIA factors (1 therm = 100,000 Btu; 1 kWh = 3,412 Btu)

values.label: EIA worked example (price per million Btu)
values.value: Natural gas at $13.66 per thousand cubic feet ÷ 1.036 = $13.18 per MMBtu; heating oil at $4.11 per gallon ÷ 0.137381 = $29.90 per MMBtu

entries.short: A rate of using or producing energy equal to 1,000 watts; running 1 kW for an hour uses 1 kilowatt-hour (kWh), the unit on your electricity bill.
entries.body: Equipment capacity and solar panels are rated in kilowatts, while your bill counts kilowatt-hours of energy. A 3.5 kW air conditioner is a one-ton unit (12,000 BTU per hour). Solar rebates are often quoted per kW of panel capacity, and an electric heater's kW rating is also how much power it draws at full output.
entries.whyItMatters: Mixing up kW and kWh is common, and keeping them straight makes solar quotes and heating and cooling specs much easier to read.

values.label: Conversions
values.value: 1 kW = 1,000 W ≈ 3,412 BTU per hour; 3.5 kW ≈ 1 ton of cooling

entries.short: Adjusting energy use for how cold or hot a period was, using degree-days, so bills from different years or homes can be compared fairly.
entries.body: A cold winter raises heating use even if nothing about the house changed, so an auditor divides heating energy by the heating degree-days for the same billing period, or scales it to a typical year. Comparing weather-normalized use before and after an upgrade shows the real savings. EIA uses degree-days the same way to model and compare energy use across months and regions.
entries.whyItMatters: Without it, a mild winter can make an upgrade look better than it is, and a harsh one can hide real savings.

values.label: Basic method
values.value: Heating use per degree-day = heating energy ÷ heating degree-days for the same billing period

entries.short: A natural radioactive gas from uranium in soil and rock that can build up in homes; long-term exposure raises the risk of lung cancer.
entries.body: You can't see, smell or taste radon, so testing is the only way to know your level. It enters through foundation cracks, sumps, floor drains and gaps around pipes, drawn in by the stack effect and depressurization. Canada and the US use different units and action levels (see radon units).
entries.whyItMatters: Air sealing and ventilation changes affect radon, so a radon test before or after upgrades belongs in any audit, and fixing high levels usually costs about as much as other common home repairs.

values.label: Health Canada guideline
values.value: 200 Bq/m³ (annual average in a normally occupied area); act within 1 year if above, sooner if much higher, and keep levels as low as reasonably achievable

values.label: US EPA action level
values.value: 4 pCi/L (EPA rounds it to 150 Bq/m³); consider fixing between 2 and 4 pCi/L

values.label: Average US levels (EPA)
values.value: About 1.3 pCi/L indoors (≈ 50 Bq/m³); about 0.4 pCi/L outdoors (≈ 15 Bq/m³)

values.label: Canadian homes above the guideline
values.value: 6.9% of Canadians in Health Canada's 2009–2011 survey; a 2024 study cited by Health Canada found 17.8% of houses at or above 200 Bq/m³

values.label: US homes with elevated radon (EPA, 2009)
values.value: Nearly 1 in 15

entries.caNote: Health Canada's guideline is 200 Bq/m³; use a long-term test of at least 91 days, ideally during the heating season.
entries.usNote: EPA's action level is 4 pCi/L; a short-term test is a common first screen, followed by a long-term or second short-term test before deciding.

entries.short: Canada measures radon in becquerels per cubic metre (Bq/m³) and the US in picocuries per litre (pCi/L); 1 pCi/L equals 37 Bq/m³.
entries.shortUs: The US measures radon in picocuries per liter (pCi/L) and Canada in becquerels per cubic meter (Bq/m³); 1 pCi/L equals 37 Bq/m³.
entries.body: Both units describe how many radioactive decays happen in a volume of air. To convert, multiply pCi/L by 37 to get Bq/m³, or divide Bq/m³ by 37 to get pCi/L. Health Canada's 200 Bq/m³ guideline is about 5.4 pCi/L, while EPA's 4 pCi/L action level is about 148 Bq/m³, so the US level is lower.
entries.whyItMatters: Test kits and lab reports may use either unit, and converting correctly tells you which guideline your result falls under.

values.label: Conversion
values.value: 1 pCi/L = 37 Bq/m³ exactly (1 curie = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ becquerels)

values.label: Health Canada guideline in US units
values.value: 200 Bq/m³ ≈ 5.4 pCi/L

values.label: EPA action level in metric units
values.value: 4 pCi/L = 148 Bq/m³ (EPA rounds to 150)

values.label: EPA 'consider fixing' level
values.value: 2 pCi/L = 74 Bq/m³ (EPA rounds to 75)

entries.short: Fixing high radon, usually with a pipe through the basement floor and a fan that pulls soil gas from under the slab and vents it outside.
entries.body: Sub-slab depressurization makes the pressure under the floor lower than in the house, so soil gas is drawn into the pipe instead of indoors. Sealing cracks and sumps helps but isn't enough on its own, and an HRV gives only modest reductions. The fan runs continuously, and a follow-up test confirms the fix.
entries.whyItMatters: Mitigation is usually affordable and very effective, and it's easiest to plan alongside basement air sealing or renovations.

values.label: Cost (Health Canada, 2014)
values.value: Typically $2,000–$3,000 installed, plus about $50–$75 a year for electricity

values.label: Effectiveness
values.value: Health Canada: most homes can be reduced by more than 80%; EPA: sub-slab suction cuts levels 50%–99%

values.label: Exhaust placement (EPA)
values.value: Vent above the roof and at least 10 feet above the ground

values.label: Testing afterwards, Canada
values.value: Short-term test at least 24 hours after the fan starts, then a 3-month test the next fall or winter; long-term re-tests within 2 years, then every 5 years

values.label: Testing afterwards, US
values.value: Within 30 days of installation but not sooner than 24 hours, using a 2–7 day test; retest at least every 2 years

values.label: Install time and cost (Health Canada, page modified 2026-09-22)
values.value: Usually installed in less than a day, for about the same cost as other common home repairs

entries.caNote: Health Canada recommends hiring a professional certified under the Canadian National Radon Proficiency Program (C-NRPP) and having the follow-up long-term test done independently of the installer.
entries.usNote: EPA suggests checking with your state radon office for licensed or certified contractors and getting an independent follow-up test.

entries.short: Measuring radon with a detector left in the home; long-term tests, over 90 days, give the most reliable yearly average.
entries.body: Short-term tests last 2 to 90 days and give a quick snapshot, but radon rises and falls with weather and season. Long-term tests run more than 90 days; Health Canada recommends at least 91 days, ideally 3 to 12 months including the heating season. Place the detector in a regularly used room on the lowest lived-in level, away from kitchens, bathrooms, drafts and the floor.
entries.whyItMatters: Mitigation decisions should rest on a reliable average, and a retest after air sealing or a new HRV shows whether radon changed.

values.label: Health Canada
values.value: At least 91 days, with 91+ days in the heating season; device about 30 cm (1 ft) above the floor and from walls; passive short-term devices aren't suitable for mitigation decisions; hourly readings above 200 Bq/m³ can occur naturally

values.label: US EPA
values.value: Short-term 2–90 days; long-term over 90 days; if a short-term result is 4 pCi/L or more, follow up with a long-term or second short-term test; place the kit at least 20 inches above the floor

entries.caNote: Health Canada says to base decisions on a long-term test, not a passive short-term kit, and on the longest representative average from an electronic monitor rather than hourly spikes.
entries.usNote: EPA's approach is a short-term test first, then a follow-up long-term or second short-term test before deciding to fix.
entries.bodyUs: Short-term tests last 2 to 90 days and give a quick snapshot, but radon rises and falls with weather and season. Long-term tests run more than 90 days and give a better picture of your yearly average. Place the detector in a regularly used room on the lowest lived-in level, away from kitchens, bathrooms, drafts and the floor.

entries.short: Fungi that grow on damp surfaces indoors; they can damage materials and affect health, and moisture is always the root cause.
entries.body: Mould needs moisture, so it appears where there are leaks, condensation or high relative humidity: basements, bathrooms, window frames, attics and cold walls behind furniture. A musty smell can be a sign even when you can't see it. Small areas can usually be cleaned by homeowners; large or recurring growth needs a professional and a fix for the moisture source.
entries.bodyUs: Mold needs moisture, so it appears where there are leaks, condensation or high relative humidity: basements, bathrooms, window frames, attics and cold walls behind furniture. A musty smell can be a sign even when you can't see it. Small areas can usually be cleaned by homeowners; large or recurring growth needs a professional and a fix for the moisture source.
entries.whyItMatters: Auditors look for mould and moisture because sealing or insulating over a damp area can make it worse, so moisture problems are fixed first.
entries.whyUs: Auditors look for mold and moisture because sealing or insulating over a damp area can make it worse, so moisture problems are fixed first.

values.label: Size categories (Health Canada)
values.value: Small: up to 3 patches, each under 1 m²; medium: more than 3 patches or patches of 1–3 m²; extensive: a patch over 3 m² (consider a professional)

values.label: Humidity to discourage mold (EPA)
values.value: Below 60%, ideally 30%–50%

entries.caNote: Health Canada says small and medium areas can generally be cleaned yourself, and to get professional help for extensive or recurring mould.

entries.short: How clean and healthy the air inside a home is, affected by ventilation, humidity, combustion gases, particles, chemicals and radon.
entries.body: Common indoor pollutants include carbon monoxide, fine particles (PM2.5) from cooking, smoking and wildfire smoke, VOCs from products and furnishings, radon, and mould from excess moisture. The main tools are controlling sources, ventilation (exhaust fans, an HRV or ERV) and filtration (see MERV).
entries.bodyUs: Common indoor pollutants include carbon monoxide, fine particles (PM2.5) from cooking, smoking and wildfire smoke, VOCs from products and furnishings, radon, and mold from excess moisture. The main tools are controlling sources, ventilation (exhaust fans, an HRV or ERV) and filtration (see MERV).
entries.whyItMatters: Energy upgrades change how air moves through a house, so a good audit checks indoor air quality risks before and after air sealing.

values.label: Health Canada humidity guidance
values.value: Keep relative humidity between 30% and 50%

entries.caNote: Health Canada also recommends at least one certified CO alarm next to sleeping areas and extra ventilation during painting or renovation.

entries.short: Chemicals that evaporate into the air from paints, glues, cleaning products, new furniture, flooring and some building materials.
entries.body: Formaldehyde is one of the best-known VOCs and has its own Health Canada guideline. Levels are highest after renovations or when new materials go in, and in tight homes with too little ventilation. Choosing low-emission products, ventilating well during and after projects, and storing fuels and solvents outside the house reduce exposure.
entries.whyItMatters: Insulation, sealants and renovation products can release VOCs, so ventilation planning belongs in any upgrade plan.

values.label: Health Canada formaldehyde guideline
values.value: 123 µg/m³ (100 ppb) averaged over 1 hour; 50 µg/m³ (40 ppb) over 8 hours

entries.caNote: Health Canada notes most air cleaners remove particles, not gases, so they're not a full answer for VOCs; ventilation is.
entries.bodyUs: Formaldehyde is one of the best-known VOCs. Levels are highest after renovations or when new materials go in, and in tight homes with too little ventilation. Choosing low-emission products, ventilating well during and after projects, and storing fuels and solvents outside the house reduce exposure.

entries.short: Fine, inhalable airborne particles 2.5 microns or smaller, from smoke, cooking, candles and outdoor pollution.
entries.body: Indoor PM2.5 comes from cooking, smoking, candles, wood burning and outdoor air leaking in, especially during wildfire smoke. Range hoods vented outdoors, a better furnace filter (see MERV) and portable air cleaners lower it. Low-cost sensors give a rough reading in micrograms per cubic metre (µg/m³).
entries.bodyUs: Indoor PM2.5 comes from cooking, smoking, candles, wood burning and outdoor air leaking in, especially during wildfire smoke. Range hoods vented outdoors, a better furnace filter (see MERV) and portable air cleaners lower it. Low-cost sensors give a rough reading in micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³).
entries.whyItMatters: Tightening a home keeps outdoor smoke out but can trap particles made indoors, so ventilation and filtration should be part of the plan.

values.label: Health Canada (indoor)
values.value: No numerical limit; keep levels as low as possible and below outdoor levels

values.label: WHO 2021 air quality guideline
values.value: 5 µg/m³ annual mean; 15 µg/m³ 24-hour mean

values.label: US EPA outdoor standard (NAAQS, page updated Oct 21, 2026)
values.value: 9.0 µg/m³ annual; 35 µg/m³ 24-hour

entries.short: A mineral fibre once common in building products; low risk when left intact, but dangerous to breathe when materials are damaged or removed.
entries.shortUs: A mineral fiber once common in building products; low risk when left intact, but dangerous to breathe when materials are damaged or removed.
entries.body: Homes built before 1990 may contain asbestos in pipe and boiler insulation, vermiculite attic insulation, floor and ceiling tiles, plaster, drywall compounds, siding and roofing. You can't tell by looking; a lab test of a sample is needed. Canada banned the import, sale and use of asbestos and most asbestos products in 2018.
entries.whyItMatters: Suspected asbestos changes the scope, order and cost of insulation and renovation work, so audits flag it before anything is disturbed.

values.label: Canada (Health Canada)
values.value: Mainly used in insulating buildings before 1990; 2018 regulations prohibit its import, sale and use, with limited exclusions

entries.caNote: Health Canada advises hiring a professional to test before renovating and a qualified removal specialist if asbestos is found.
entries.usNote: EPA advises treating vermiculite attic insulation as asbestos-containing and leaving any removal to professionals.
entries.bodyUs: Homes built before 1990 may contain asbestos in pipe and boiler insulation, vermiculite attic insulation, floor and ceiling tiles, plaster, drywall compounds, siding and roofing. You can't tell by looking; a lab test of a sample is needed.

entries.short: Paint containing lead, common in older homes; sanding, scraping or removing it creates toxic dust that's especially harmful to young children.
entries.body: In Canada, homes built before 1960 probably contain lead paint and those from 1960 to 1990 may have it on exterior surfaces. In the US, the key date is 1978. Intact paint out of children's reach is often safer left alone; work that disturbs it, including window replacement, needs lead-safe methods.
entries.whyItMatters: Window and door replacement and other energy upgrades can disturb old paint, so contractors need to plan for it.

values.label: Canada (Health Canada)
values.value: Before 1960: probably contains lead paint; 1960–1990: exterior paint may; after 1990: virtually lead-free

values.label: US EPA RRP rule
values.value: Covers homes built before 1978; minor work disturbing 6 ft² or less per room inside or 20 ft² or less outside is exempt; window replacement is always covered

entries.caNote: Health Canada says there's no known safe level of lead exposure and advises against sanders, heat guns and torches on lead paint.
entries.usNote: Contractors paid to disturb paint in pre-1978 homes must be certified under EPA's Renovation, Repair and Painting (RRP) program and follow its work practices, except for small jobs under the size limits.
entries.bodyCa: In Canada, homes built before 1960 probably contain lead paint and those from 1960 to 1990 may have it on exterior surfaces. Intact paint out of children's reach is often safer left alone; work that disturbs it, including window replacement, needs lead-safe methods.
entries.bodyUs: In the US, the key date is 1978: homes built before then may contain lead-based paint. Intact paint out of children's reach is often safer left alone; work that disturbs it, including window replacement, needs lead-safe methods.

entries.short: Lab testing of water from a private well for bacteria and chemicals, done on a regular schedule and after floods or repairs.
entries.body: Basic tests look for coliform bacteria, including E. coli, which signal contamination from the surface or from sewage. Which chemicals to test for, and how often, depends on local geology and land use, so ask your local public health unit or state agency. Follow the lab's sampling instructions.
entries.whyItMatters: A home health screen flags whether a well test is due, especially before buying, after flooding, or when someone in the household is vulnerable.

values.label: Health Canada
values.value: Test for microbes at least every 6 months (early spring and fall, and after heavy rain, floods, fire, drought or long disuse); general water quality every 2 years

values.label: Safe microbial result (Health Canada)
values.value: No E. coli and no total coliforms per 100 mL

values.label: Safe microbial result (EPA)
values.value: No E. coli and no total coliforms per 100 mL

values.label: US EPA
values.value: Test at least once a year for total coliform bacteria, nitrates, total dissolved solids and pH; more often with infants, older adults, or pregnant or nursing household members

entries.bodyCa: Basic tests look for coliform bacteria, including E. coli, which signal contamination from the surface or from sewage. Which chemicals to test for, and how often, depends on local geology and land use, so ask your local public health unit. Follow the lab's sampling instructions.
entries.bodyUs: Basic tests look for coliform bacteria, including E. coli, which signal contamination from the surface or from sewage. Which chemicals to test for, and how often, depends on local geology and land use, so ask your local or state health department. Follow the lab's sampling instructions.

entries.short: Bacteria used as warning signs in well water: total coliforms point to surface contamination, and E. coli to contamination from sewage or manure.
entries.body: Total coliforms are used as an indicator that germs could be getting into the well. E. coli comes from human or animal waste, so finding it means the water isn't safe to drink until the well is fixed, disinfected and retested. Results are reported per 100 mL of water.
entries.whyItMatters: A positive result means treating or disinfecting the well and retesting before relying on the water.

values.label: Health Canada safe result
values.value: None detected: no E. coli and no total coliforms in a 100 mL sample

values.label: Safe result (EPA)
values.value: None detected: no E. coli and no total coliforms in a 100 mL sample

entries.short: Canada's certification program for radon professionals; Health Canada recommends a C-NRPP certified professional to fix high radon.
entries.body: C-NRPP certifies radon professionals, including the contractors who design and install radon reduction systems, and its certified professionals are trained on the Canadian standard for that work. It also runs performance testing for radon monitors. You can look up certified professionals in its online directory.
entries.whyItMatters: A radon fix is only as good as its installation, so checking for C-NRPP certification is the simplest way to vet a mitigation contractor or a test provider.

values.label: Health Canada advice on fixing radon (page modified 2026-09-22)
values.value: Hire a contractor certified as a radon mitigation professional under C-NRPP

values.label: Health Canada advice on do-it-yourself testing (page modified 2025-09-04)
values.value: For a long-term test with an electronic monitor, choose one that has passed C-NRPP performance testing; tests should run at least 3 months

entries.short: Professional work to remove, seal or enclose a hazard such as asbestos, mould or lead paint, and to clean up safely afterward.
entries.shortUs: Professional work to remove, seal or enclose a hazard such as asbestos, mold or lead paint, and to clean up safely afterward.
entries.body: Abatement usually refers to asbestos or lead: trained crews contain the work area so dust can't spread, then remove the material or permanently seal or enclose it. Remediation is the usual word for mould: removing contaminated materials, cleaning the rest and fixing the moisture source. Painting over lead paint or covering mould without fixing the cause doesn't count.
entries.bodyUs: Abatement usually refers to asbestos or lead: trained crews contain the work area so dust can't spread, then remove the material or permanently seal or enclose it. Remediation is the usual word for mold: removing contaminated materials, cleaning the rest and fixing the moisture source. Painting over lead paint or covering mold without fixing the cause doesn't count.
entries.whyItMatters: Hazard work is quoted separately from testing and has to be finished before insulation or air sealing goes ahead in that area, so it affects both the order and the cost of an upgrade plan.

values.label: Health Canada (asbestos)
values.value: Hire a professional to test before renovating, and a qualified asbestos removal specialist if asbestos is found

values.label: Health Canada (mould)
values.value: Get professional help for extensive mould (a patch over 3 m²) or mould that keeps coming back

values.label: US EPA (lead)
values.value: Abatement permanently addresses lead hazards and must be done by certified individuals and firms; painting over doesn't qualify

entries.short: A foam insulation pumped into wall cavities in the 1970s that released formaldehyde gas; foamed-in-place UFFI has been prohibited in Canada since 1980.
entries.body: UFFI was installed by drilling holes and filling wall cavities with a foam that hardened in place. It was used mainly in the 1970s, and Canada prohibited foamed-in-place UFFI in 1980 over health concerns about formaldehyde.
entries.whyItMatters: Buyers and insurers may ask about UFFI, so it's worth noting if an inspection or audit finds signs of it in the walls.

values.label: Status in Canada (NRCan)
values.value: Foamed-in-place UFFI prohibited since 1980

entries.short: The public health area a radon survey reports by, such as a BC Health Service Delivery Area; results describe a region, not your home.
entries.body: Health Canada's 2009–2011 cross-Canada survey placed three-month radon tests in about 14,000 homes across all 121 health regions, which are areas served by a hospital board or regional health authority and defined by each province. The share of homes above the guideline varied widely: it was 23%–44% in 14 regions. Because each region's figure comes from about 100 homes or fewer, a low regional figure doesn't mean your home is low.
entries.whyItMatters: Regional radon numbers show how common high levels are near you, but only a test of your own home tells you your level.

values.label: Health Canada cross-Canada survey (final report, 2012)
values.value: 13,807 valid long-term results from 121 health regions; 6.9% of Canadians lived in homes above 200 Bq/m³

values.label: Example (BC)
values.value: Fraser East Health Service Delivery Area: 3.0% of 100 homes tested were above 200 Bq/m³

entries.short: The radon level at which agencies advise fixing a home: 200 Bq/m³ in Canada (Health Canada) and 4 pCi/L in the US (EPA).
entries.shortCa: Health Canada's radon guideline: fix your home if the yearly average where people spend time is above 200 Bq/m³, within a year, and sooner if higher.
entries.shortUs: EPA's radon action level: fix your home if testing shows 4 pCi/L or more, and consider fixing it between 2 and 4 pCi/L.
entries.body: Health Canada's guideline applies to the average annual level in a normal occupancy area, meaning any part of the home where someone spends more than 4 hours a day, and it also asks for levels as low as reasonably achievable. EPA's action level of 4 pCi/L, about 150 Bq/m³, is lower than Canada's guideline, so the same result can mean fix it now in the US and keep watching in Canada. Both agencies say lower is better.
entries.whyItMatters: Your test result is compared with these levels to decide whether a radon mitigation system is needed and how soon.

values.label: Canada (Health Canada, page modified 2025-09-24)
values.value: 200 Bq/m³ annual average in the normal occupancy area; act within 1 year, sooner the higher the level

values.label: US (EPA)
values.value: Fix at 4 pCi/L or more; consider fixing between 2 and 4 pCi/L

values.label: Same result, two answers
values.value: 150 Bq/m³ (about 4 pCi/L) is above EPA's action level but below Health Canada's guideline

entries.bodyUs: EPA recommends fixing your home if radon is 4 pCi/L or more, and considering a fix between 2 and 4 pCi/L, because no level is risk-free. Canada's guideline is higher, 200 Bq/m³ (about 5.4 pCi/L), so the same result can mean fix it now in the US and keep watching in Canada.

entries.short: EPA's 1993 county map of radon potential, from Zone 1 (highest) to Zone 3 (lowest); EPA says not to use it to decide whether to test.
entries.body: Zone 1 counties have the highest potential, with predicted average indoor levels that may exceed 4 pCi/L; Zone 2 is moderate (2 to 4 pCi/L) and Zone 3 low (under 2 pCi/L). The map was made to help put radon-resistant building codes in place, and homes with high radon have been found in all three zones.
entries.whyItMatters: A low zone doesn't make your house safe, so treat the zone as background and rely on a test of your own home.

values.label: Zones (EPA)
values.value: Zone 1: may be greater than 4 pCi/L; Zone 2: 2–4 pCi/L; Zone 3: less than 2 pCi/L (predicted average indoor levels)

entries.short: A chemical from fertilizer, manure and sewage that can seep into wells; high levels are dangerous for babies, so test well water for it.
entries.body: You can't see nitrate in water, so only a lab test shows the level. Infants are most at risk: high levels reduce the blood's ability to carry oxygen, a condition known as blue baby syndrome. Wells near fields, livestock or septic systems are more likely to be affected.
entries.whyItMatters: If a baby or pregnant person lives in the home, a nitrate test belongs alongside the regular bacteria test, especially in farm areas.

entries.short: A very fine high-efficiency particulate air filter used in portable air cleaners and vacuums to trap smoke, dust and other small particles.
entries.body: Portable air cleaners often reach a high clean air delivery rate (CADR) by using a HEPA filter, and some studies have found small health improvements from using them. A HEPA vacuum traps fine dust instead of blowing it back into the room.
entries.whyItMatters: During wildfire smoke or renovation dust, a correctly sized HEPA air cleaner is one of the quickest ways to lower fine particles indoors.

values.label: Sizing a portable air cleaner (EPA)
values.value: Minimum CADR of about 65 cfm for 100 ft², 130 for 200 ft² and 195 for 300 ft² (8-foot ceilings)

entries.short: A handheld X-ray fluorescence instrument that measures lead in paint through the layers, without scraping off samples, during a lead inspection.
entries.body: A certified inspector holds the XRF against painted surfaces throughout the home to find where lead-based paint is. It's faster and less damaging than cutting out paint chips for a lab.
entries.whyItMatters: An XRF inspection tells you which windows, doors and trim contain lead before replacement or other upgrades disturb them.

entries.short: An early type of house wiring that runs separate wires on porcelain knobs and through porcelain tubes, with no ground wire; insulation must not cover it.
entries.body: It's found in many older homes, often still live in attics and walls. NRCan warns never to let insulation touch old knob-and-tube wiring, because it can pose a fire hazard. Have a licensed electrician assess it before anyone air seals or insulates the attic or walls.
entries.whyItMatters: Finding knob-and-tube changes the order of work: the wiring has to be assessed, and often replaced, before attic or wall insulation can go in.

values.label: NRCan insulation safety rule
values.value: Never let insulation contact old knob-and-tube wiring, a chimney or a combustion vent

entries.bodyUs: It's found in many older homes, often still live in attics and walls. Insulation shouldn't bury live knob-and-tube wiring, because the wires were designed to shed heat into open air; the national electrical code generally doesn't allow it to be covered by loose, rolled or blown insulation. Have a licensed electrician assess it before anyone air seals or insulates the attic or walls.

entries.short: A safety inspection of a wood stove, fireplace insert or chimney by a professional certified through WETT, Canada's wood-energy training association.
entries.body: Wood Energy Technology Transfer Inc. (WETT Inc.) is a non-profit training and education association that serves as the national registrar for WETT-certified professionals. A Level 1 inspection is visual and covers most insurance and real estate needs; Levels 2 and 3 go further, with tools and, if needed, opening walls or chimneys. You get an official inspection report, not a certificate.
entries.whyItMatters: Insurers often ask for one when you buy a home with a wood stove or add one, and an audit that finds a wood appliance may recommend it before air sealing.

values.label: Inspection levels (WETT)
values.value: Level 1 visual (most insurance and real estate needs); Level 2 technical; Level 3 invasive

entries.short: A flammable tar that builds up inside chimneys and flue pipes when wood smoke cools and condenses; too much of it can start a chimney fire.
entries.body: Smouldering fires, wet wood and cold chimneys all increase creosote. CMHC's wood-heating guide says to check the flue often and clean it when deposits build up past about 4 mm (1/8 in.); older smoky stoves may need cleaning every few weeks, while efficient certified stoves may need it only once a year.
entries.bodyUs: Smoldering fires, wet wood and cold chimneys all increase creosote. Check the flue often and have it cleaned when deposits build up past about 1/8 inch; older smoky stoves may need cleaning every few weeks, while efficient certified stoves may need it only once a year.
entries.whyItMatters: Regular sweeping keeps a wood stove safe, and because tightening a house can change how a stove drafts, its venting is part of a combustion safety check.

values.label: When to clean (CMHC wood-heating guide)
values.value: When deposits exceed about 4 mm (1/8 in.); as often as every few weeks for older smoky systems, about once a year for advanced stoves

entries.short: The federal department that built Canada's home energy programs, like EnerGuide; its efficiency office moved to Environment and Climate Change Canada in 2026.
entries.body: NRCan's Office of Energy Efficiency created the EnerGuide Rating System and HOT2000 software, licenses service organizations, registers energy advisors and ran the Canada Greener Homes programs. Control of the Office of Energy Efficiency was transferred to Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) effective July 30, 2026, and program pages say they're transitioning. Many of those pages still sit on NRCan's website.
entries.whyItMatters: Official EnerGuide evaluations and federal home programs still run on NRCan-built systems, so you'll see the name on reports, product lists and rebate rules.

entries.short: The federal environment department, which took over NRCan's Office of Energy Efficiency, including home energy programs, on July 30, 2026.
entries.body: ECCC now announces federal home efficiency news such as new CGHAP agreements and the ENERGY STAR Canada awards, and the CGHAP and Oil to Heat Pump Affordability pages say those programs are transitioning to ECCC. ECCC also publishes the climate data, such as heating degree days, used in energy calculations.
entries.whyItMatters: For current federal home energy program information, expect it to come from ECCC even when web pages still carry NRCan's name.

entries.short: A professional registered with NRCan to do official EnerGuide home evaluations, working through a licensed service organization.
entries.body: The energy advisor visits your home, measures and inspects it, runs a blower door test, builds a HOT2000 model and produces your EnerGuide rating, label and Renovation Upgrade Report. Advisors work through a service organization licensed by NRCan. Official evaluations happen only when a homeowner requests one, and NRCan hasn't authorized anyone to contact homeowners unsolicited.
entries.whyItMatters: Canadian programs that require an evaluation, including the assessment stream of Ontario's HRSP, need a registered energy advisor's pre- and post-retrofit evaluations.

entries.short: A company licensed by NRCan to deliver EnerGuide evaluations; it employs or contracts registered energy advisors and books your visit.
entries.body: Service organizations handle scheduling, quality control and file submission, and official EnerGuide evaluations are done only through them. Some programs limit which ones you can use: Ontario's HRSP emails you a list of approved service organizations for your area, and the follow-up evaluation must be done by the same one.
entries.whyItMatters: Booking through the right service organization, and using the same one for your follow-up, keeps your rebate file valid.

values.label: Ontario HRSP assessment rebate
values.value: $600 to offset the initial and follow-up assessments

entries.term: Pre- and post-retrofit evaluations ("D" and "E" evaluations)
entries.short: The EnerGuide evaluation done before upgrades (a 'D' file) and the one done after (an 'E' file), used to verify the work for rebates.
entries.body: The pre-retrofit evaluation records your home's starting point and recommends upgrades; the post-retrofit evaluation, by the same service organization, confirms what was done and re-rates the house. NRCan's EnerGuide data labels existing-home evaluations as D (pre-retrofit) and E (post-retrofit) files.
entries.whyItMatters: Programs that use evaluations pay only once the work is confirmed in the post-retrofit evaluation, and they set firm deadlines for it.

entries.short: NRCan's energy modelling software that registered energy advisors use to calculate a home's EnerGuide rating and upgrade savings.
entries.body: The advisor enters the home's dimensions, insulation, windows, airtightness from the blower door test and mechanical systems, and HOT2000 estimates annual energy use and the effect of upgrades. The resulting file is submitted to NRCan.
entries.whyItMatters: The quality of the data entered decides how accurate your rating and projected savings are, so a thorough site visit matters.

entries.short: The personalized list of recommended upgrades, projected savings and before-and-after ratings you receive with an EnerGuide evaluation.
entries.body: It shows how your home uses energy, its heat loss by component, which upgrades the advisor recommends, and what your EnerGuide rating would be after them. It also includes energy-saving tips and the advisor's comments.
entries.whyItMatters: Use it to plan and prioritize upgrades, and keep it with your rebate paperwork.

entries.short: A federal program that pays the full cost of recommended energy upgrades for low- to median-income homeowners and renters, through provinces.
entries.body: CGHAP uses a direct-install model: a provincial partner or utility arranges the assessment and installs upgrades such as insulation, air sealing and heat pumps at no upfront cost to eligible households. You apply through your province's partner program, not the federal government, and income rules vary by province. The program is transitioning from NRCan to ECCC, and no third parties are authorized to contact homeowners about it unsolicited.
entries.whyItMatters: For eligible households it can cover what other rebates only partly fund, but it's available only where a provincial agreement is in place.

Administrators can change or end rebates without notice, and payments depend on available funding.

entries.short: An Inflation Reduction Act rebate run by states for efficient electric equipment and envelope upgrades in lower- and moderate-income homes.
entries.body: HEEHR offers point-of-sale rebates, taken off the price by participating contractors or retailers, of up to $14,000 per household for items such as heat pumps, heat pump water heaters, insulation, air sealing, ventilation and electrical upgrades, for households under 150% of area median income. It's available only where your state, territory or tribe has launched a program. DOE's May 2026 revision removed rebates for replacing gas, oil or propane equipment with electric, so HEEHR now covers electric-to-electric upgrades and new construction, and it requires insulation and air sealing before heating and cooling upgrades unless the home already meets a state-set level.
entries.whyItMatters: If you heat with fossil fuels, HEEHR may no longer cover a heat pump switch, though the HOMES rebate still can; check your state energy office for what's open.

entries.term: HOMES rebates (Home Owner Managing Energy Savings)
entries.short: A federal rebate, run by states, that pays $2,000 to $8,000 based on the modeled energy savings of whole-home upgrades.
entries.body: HOMES rewards projects by how much energy they save, with a minimum of 20% modeled savings, and covers insulation, air sealing, heating and cooling equipment, water heaters, duct sealing, appliances and lighting. It's open to all income levels, with larger rebates for lower-income households. DOE's May 2026 revision restored the law's name for the program, Home Owner Managing Energy Savings, made ENERGY STAR compliance and several state plan elements optional, and removed Justice40 requirements.
entries.whyItMatters: A HOMES project usually starts with an energy audit and model, which is exactly what an assessment provides.

Households at or below 200% of the federal poverty guidelines generally qualify (states may use 60% of state median income instead), and both owners and renters can apply. They require exams and documented experience, and Energy Auditor holders renew every five years. BPI also publishes standards such as ANSI/BPI-1100 (home energy auditing) and ANSI/BPI-1200 (basic analysis of buildings).

entries.whyItMatters: Raters often verify new homes for energy codes and programs such as ENERGY STAR and DOE Efficient New Homes, so they're the professionals behind most HERS scores you'll see.

Many require pre-approval, a participating contractor, proof of purchase and sometimes the equipment's AHRI certificate or an energy assessment; some are instant discounts through the store or contractor.
entries.whyItMatters: Rebates change the payback of upgrades, so check them before signing; some must be applied for before work starts.

Tariffed versions attach the charge to the meter, so it can pass to the next owner or tenant, while loans usually stay with the borrower.
entries.whyItMatters: It can make upgrades possible without upfront cash, but missed payments can lead to utility disconnection, so read the terms.

entries.body: A municipality, or its program partner, pays for approved upgrades and recovers the cost through your property taxes over many years, and the charge can transfer to a buyer when you sell. Terms, interest rates and eligible upgrades vary by program.
entries.whyItMatters: It can spread the cost of big projects like heat pumps or insulation over their useful life, but it's still debt secured on your home, so compare rates and fees.

entries.short: Canada's main standards organization; building codes, rebates and product labels often point to its standards, such as F280 for heating system sizing.
entries.body: CSA Group, the Canadian Standards Association, writes many of the standards that Canadian codes, rebate programs and equipment certifications refer to. Two you'll meet around an audit are CSA F280, the method for sizing heating and cooling equipment (see heat-loss calculation), and CSA B415.1, the test of a wood stove's heat output, efficiency and emissions.
entries.whyItMatters: When a quote or rebate rule names a CSA standard, it tells you exactly what the work or the equipment has to meet, so ask the contractor to show it.

entries.short: Canada's model building code; once a province or territory adopts it, it sets minimum insulation, ventilation and safety rules for new homes and renovations.
entries.body: The NBC is developed by the Canadian Board for Harmonized Construction Codes and published by the National Research Council, and it applies only once a province or territory adopts it, sometimes with changes. Part 9 covers houses and small buildings, and its energy rules (Section 9.36) are organized in performance tiers. The 2025 edition adds a passive radon stack for dwelling units and a new Part 10 on energy upgrades when existing buildings are altered.
entries.whyItMatters: Your province's version of the code sets the minimum insulation, ventilation and window levels for renovations and additions, and its climate zones are the ones quoted on many Canadian pages.

entries.short: Canada's national housing agency; it insures mortgages, publishes homeowner guides and refunds part of your mortgage insurance premium for energy upgrades.
entries.body: CMHC runs mortgage loan insurance and much of Canada's housing research. Its CMHC Eco Improvement program refunds 25% of the mortgage insurance premium for buyers with a CMHC-insured mortgage who complete at least $20,000 of eligible energy-saving work and apply within 2 years of closing. Its About Your House guides are also the source of common advice, such as keeping winter humidity near 30% when it's very cold outside.
entries.whyItMatters: If you bought with a CMHC-insured mortgage, an audit-backed renovation plan can also earn back part of your insurance premium, as long as you apply in time.

entries.term: Assessment path and no-assessment path (Home Renovation Savings)
entries.short: Ontario's Home Renovation Savings program has two routes: one needs home energy assessments before and after the work; the other pays set rebates without one.
entries.body: On the assessment path you book an initial EnerGuide assessment with an approved service organization, complete at least two recommended upgrades, then have a final assessment with the same energy advisor. It pays for insulation, windows and doors, air sealing and heat pump water heaters, plus $600 toward the two assessments and a $500 bonus for three upgrades. The no-assessment path pays fixed rebates for heat pumps, attic insulation, smart thermostats, appliances and solar with batteries, usually through participating contractors and with pre-approval for heat pumps and solar.
entries.whyItMatters: Choosing a path decides whether you need an EnerGuide assessment first, and the assessment path's follow-up must be scheduled by November 30, 2026 and completed by December 31, 2026.

entries.short: Yearly income figures, by household size, that the US government publishes and assistance programs use to set income limits, such as 200% of poverty.
entries.body: The Department of Health and Human Services updates its poverty guidelines each January, with higher figures for Alaska and Hawaii; program pages often call them the federal poverty level, or FPL. Programs set limits as a percentage of them: the Weatherization Assistance Program generally uses 200%, and LIHEAP allows up to 150% or 60% of state median income, whichever is greater.
entries.whyItMatters: Your household income as a percentage of FPL decides whether you qualify for free weatherization, bill assistance and some rebates.

entries.term: LIHEAP (Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program)
aka: Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program
entries.short: A federal program, run by states, tribes and territories, that helps lower-income households pay heating and cooling bills and avoid shutoffs.
entries.body: LIHEAP is funded by the Department of Health and Human Services and delivered locally, so benefits, income limits and application dates vary by state. It can help with bills, energy emergencies and reconnections, and states may spend up to 15% of their funds (25% with a waiver) on low-cost weatherization and energy-related repairs. You apply through your state or local office; the federal program never charges a fee or gives grants directly to individuals.
entries.whyItMatters: LIHEAP eligibility can also qualify you for weatherization and for some utility and state rebate programs, so it's worth checking even if you plan upgrades.

values.label: Federal income limit
values.value: Up to the greater of 150% of the poverty guidelines or 60% of state median income; states set their own limits but can't exclude households below 110% of poverty

values.label: Automatic eligibility
values.value: Households receiving TANF, SSI, SNAP or certain veterans' benefits can qualify regardless of income

entries.short: The middle household income for a whole state; LIHEAP and some weatherization and rebate programs set income limits as a share of it, such as 60% of SMI.
entries.body: Half of a state's households earn more than the state median income and half earn less. Federal law lets LIHEAP use the greater of 150% of the poverty guidelines or 60% of SMI, and some state weatherization and rebate programs use SMI too. Area median income (AMI) is the same idea for a county or metro area.
entries.whyItMatters: In higher-income states the 60% of SMI limit can be more generous than the poverty-based one, so check both when you see an income table.

values.label: LIHEAP federal limit
values.value: The greater of 150% of the poverty guidelines or 60% of state median income

entries.short: Qualifying for an assistance or rebate program automatically because your household already receives certain benefits, such as SNAP, SSI or TANF.
entries.body: Instead of checking your income, a program accepts proof that someone in the household gets another means-tested benefit. Federal law does this for LIHEAP with TANF, SSI, SNAP and certain veterans' benefits, and DOE's weatherization rules count households where someone received TANF or SSI cash assistance in the past 12 months. Many utility and state rebate programs publish their own lists of qualifying benefits.
entries.whyItMatters: It can save you from gathering income paperwork and often gets you into free weatherization or larger rebates faster.

entries.short: The US trade association for heating and cooling contractors that publishes the standard Manual J, S and D methods for sizing systems and ducts.
entries.body: ACCA publishes ANSI-recognized standards that US codes and rebate programs point to: Manual J for heating and cooling loads, Manual S for equipment selection and Manual D for duct design. It also co-sponsors ASHRAE's Standard 211 for commercial building energy audits.
entries.whyItMatters: When a quote or rebate rule mentions ACCA, the contractor should follow these published sizing methods, so ask to see the calculations.

aka: American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers
entries.short: An international society of heating, cooling and ventilation engineers whose standards define things like commercial energy audit levels and climate zones.
entries.body: ASHRAE (the American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers) has more than 50,000 members. Its Standard 211, co-sponsored by ACCA, sets the procedures for commercial building energy audits at Levels 1, 2 and 3, and its climate data underlie the US energy code's climate zone map.
entries.whyItMatters: For commercial buildings, the ASHRAE audit level in a quote tells you how deep the analysis goes, so compare quotes at the same level.

values.value: Standard for Commercial Building Energy Audits: defines Energy Audit Levels 1, 2 and 3

entries.short: The model US energy code for new homes and additions, updated about every three years; states and cities adopt an edition, often with changes.
entries.body: The International Code Council develops the IECC through a consensus process and typically publishes a new edition every three years, such as 2021 and 2024. It sets minimum insulation, window, airtightness, duct and equipment requirements, and its climate zone map is used across US building guidance. DOE estimated that the 2024 edition saves about 7.8% of site energy compared with the edition before it.
entries.whyItMatters: The edition your state or city has adopted sets the minimum insulation, airtightness and window levels for additions and major renovations.

entries.short: A Statistics Canada metro area: a core city plus surrounding municipalities, with at least 100,000 people in total and at least 50,000 in the core.
entries.body: Statistics Canada adds neighbouring municipalities to a CMA when enough of their residents commute into the core, so a CMA usually reaches well past city limits. Smaller areas with a core of at least 10,000 people are census agglomerations (CAs). Radon surveys, housing data and energy statistics are often reported by CMA.
entries.whyItMatters: When a statistic on a city page is for the CMA, it describes the wider metro area, which can differ from your own neighbourhood or town.

values.label: Definition (Statistics Canada, 2021 Census)
values.value: Total population of at least 100,000 with at least 50,000 in the core; census agglomerations need a core of at least 10,000

entries.short: The US government's metro area definition: counties tied by commuting to an urban core of at least 50,000 people (an MSA) or 10,000 (a micro area).
entries.body: The Office of Management and Budget delineates core-based statistical areas (CBSAs) from Census Bureau data, using counties as building blocks. An outlying county joins when enough of its residents commute to or from the central counties, so a metro area spans many cities and suburbs. Population and housing statistics for a metro are often reported for the whole CBSA.
entries.whyItMatters: A metro-wide number can hide big local differences, so treat it as context rather than a description of your neighborhood.

values.label: Definitions (Census Bureau)
values.value: Metropolitan statistical area: at least one urban area of 50,000 or more; micropolitan: 10,000 to under 50,000; CBSA covers both

entries.short: The Census Bureau's ongoing yearly household survey, the main source for local figures like home age, heating fuel, income and home ownership.
entries.body: Because the ACS surveys a sample of households every year instead of counting everyone, its figures are estimates with margins of error. Data for smaller places are usually published as five-year estimates, such as 2020–2024.
entries.whyItMatters: When a metro page says what share of homes were built before 1980 or heat with gas, that's an ACS estimate, which helps you judge how typical your house is.

entries.short: The US federal energy department, which sets appliance efficiency standards and funds home energy rebates and weatherization through the states.
entries.body: DOE writes the minimum efficiency standards for furnaces, heat pumps, air conditioners and water heaters, and it runs the Home Energy Score and its new-home program. It funds the HOMES and HEEHR rebates and the Weatherization Assistance Program, which states deliver, and it is taking over ENERGY STAR from EPA. Its national laboratories, such as PNNL, produce much of the building research audits rely on.
entries.whyItMatters: Many of the rebate rules, test procedures and efficiency ratings in a US audit report come from DOE, so its name signals the federal baseline.

entries.short: The US government's energy statistics agency, the usual source for state electricity, natural gas, heating oil and propane prices.
entries.body: EIA collects and publishes data on energy prices, production and use, including average residential prices by state. It also publishes standard conversion factors, such as 3,412 BTU per kilowatt-hour and 100,000 BTU per therm, used to compare fuels.
entries.whyItMatters: When a page estimates energy costs from EIA prices, it's using statewide averages, so your own utility rate may differ.

entries.short: A US Department of Energy national laboratory whose building research includes the Building America Solution Center and county climate zone data.
entries.body: PNNL is one of DOE's national laboratories. It hosts the Building America Solution Center, a free library of building science and testing guides, and publishes the county-by-county climate zone files used with the US energy code.
entries.whyItMatters: When a page cites PNNL for your climate zone or a testing procedure, it's pointing to DOE's own building research.

entries.short: A city loan for home energy upgrades that you repay through your property tax bill; Toronto and Saskatoon both run programs with this name.
entries.body: Toronto's HELP lends up to $125,000, or 10% of the home's current value assessment if that's less, at fixed rates over 5 to 20 years, repaid in instalments with your property taxes. Most Toronto projects need an EnerGuide evaluation before and after the work, but heat-pump-only and rooftop-solar-only projects don't. Saskatoon's HELP also offers low-interest loans repaid on the tax bill, with its own limits.
entries.whyItMatters: HELP can spread the cost of big upgrades over up to 20 years, which makes larger projects possible before rebates come back.

entries.short: The US energy code's climate map: zones 0 (hottest) to 8 (coldest), plus a moisture letter — A for moist, B for dry, C for marine.
entries.body: The International Energy Conservation Code (IECC) assigns every US county a zone number, based mainly on heating and cooling degree days, and a moisture letter. The 2021 IECC adopted the ASHRAE 169-2013 map, which added a zone 0 (not found in the US) and moved about 400 counties, mostly to warmer zones. Energy codes and ENERGY STAR insulation advice are keyed to these zones.
entries.whyItMatters: Your zone sets recommended insulation levels, window criteria and airtightness targets, and signals whether you need a cold-climate heat pump.

values.label: Zones and moisture regimes
values.value: Zones 0–8; A = moist, B = dry, C = marine (2021 IECC, based on ASHRAE 169-2013)

values.label: Building America mapping
values.value: Cold = zones 5–6 (about 5,400–9,000 HDD, °F); very cold = zone 7 (9,000–12,600); subarctic = zone 8 (12,600 or more)

values.label: Cold-climate heat pump scope (NEEP)
values.value: Zone 4 and colder

entries.short: Canada's building code climate zones, set by heating degree days: zone 4 (mildest) to zone 8 (coldest), with zone 7 split into 7A and 7B.
entries.body: The National Building Code and the National Energy Code for Buildings group locations by annual heating degree days below 18°C, and energy requirements such as insulation levels get stricter in colder zones. Provinces adopt or adapt these codes, and some publish their own zone maps.
entries.whyItMatters: Your zone sets code-minimum insulation and window levels for renovations and additions and helps size heating equipment.

values.label: Code example: Edmonton new homes (NBC(AE) 2023 prescriptive path)
values.value: Attic ceiling RSI 10.43 (R-59) without an HRV or RSI 8.67 (R-49) with one; windows U-value 1.61 W/m²·K or less

entries.caNote: NRCan's older retrofit guide, Keeping the Heat In, uses its own zones A–D for insulation advice; these don't match the NBC zones.

entries.short: Whether a place needs more energy for heating or for cooling over a year, which changes which upgrades and equipment matter most.
entries.body: Heating-dominated climates, such as nearly all of Canada and the northern US, have far more heating degree days than cooling degree days; cooling-dominated climates, such as the US Gulf Coast and desert Southwest, are the reverse, and mixed climates need both. Priorities shift accordingly: insulation, air sealing and cold-climate heat pumps in the north; shading, low-SHGC windows, duct sealing and high SEER2 in the south.
entries.whyItMatters: Advice written for one climate can be wrong for another, for example on radiant barriers and vapour barriers, so make sure guidance matches your region.
entries.whyUs: Advice written for one climate can be wrong for another, for example on radiant barriers and vapor barriers, so make sure guidance matches your region.

values.label: Building America regions (DOE)
values.value: Mixed-humid and mixed-dry: about 5,400 HDD (°F) or fewer with cold winter months; cold: 5,400–9,000; very cold: 9,000–12,600

values.label: US regional AC standards
values.value: 'North' = states with 5,000+ population-weighted heating degree days; Southeast and Southwest have higher minimum SEER2

entries.short: A climate with long, hot, muggy summers, like the US Gulf Coast and Florida, where controlling humidity matters as much as temperature.
entries.body: DOE's Building America program defines it as more than 20 inches (50 cm) of rain a year plus many hours of high humidity during the warmest six months. Homes there benefit from properly sized cooling, sealed ducts and low-SHGC windows, and should avoid interior vapor barriers that can trap moisture.
entries.whyItMatters: Cold-climate habits, such as interior polyethylene vapor barriers, can cause moisture damage in hot-humid homes.

values.label: Building America definition
values.value: Over 20 in. (50 cm) of annual precipitation and a wet-bulb temperature of 67°F (19.5°C) or more for 3,000+ hours, or 73°F (23°C) or more for 1,500+ hours, during the warmest six consecutive months

values.label: IECC equivalent
values.value: Zones 1A–3A below the warm-humid line

entries.short: A mild coastal climate with cool, wet winters and dry summers, like the US Pacific Northwest and coastal British Columbia.
entries.body: Building America defines it by a coldest-month average between −3°C and 18°C (27–65°F), a warmest month under 22°C (72°F), at least four months averaging above 10°C (50°F), and a wet winter with a dry summer. In the IECC it's the 'C' moisture regime. Homes face long, damp heating seasons more than extreme cold.
entries.whyItMatters: Moisture management, ventilation and rainscreen walls matter a lot here, and heat pumps run very efficiently in these mild winters.

values.label: Building America definition
values.value: Coldest month mean −3°C to 18°C (27–65°F); warmest month mean under 22°C (72°F); 4+ months above 10°C (50°F); wettest cold-season month gets at least 3 times the rain of the driest month of the rest of the year

values.label: IECC equivalent
values.value: Zones 3C and 4C

entries.caNote: Canada's codes don't use a 'marine' label, but coastal British Columbia has this climate pattern.

entries.short: Thirty-year averages of temperature, degree-days, precipitation and other weather at a station, used as the typical climate for a place.
entries.body: Weather agencies update normals each decade: the current sets cover 1991–2020, published by NOAA in the US and by Environment and Climate Change Canada in Canada. Calculators and audit reports use them for typical heating and cooling degree-days, so one unusual year doesn't skew the estimate. Some Canadian figures still come from the older 1981–2010 normals.
entries.whyItMatters: When a page says a city gets about 4,000 heating degree-days a year, that's a climate normal, so your own year can run colder or warmer.

values.label: US (NOAA)
values.value: 1991–2020 U.S. Climate Normals: 30-year normals at more than 15,000 stations, over 7,300 of them with temperature normals

values.label: Canada (ECCC)
values.value: 1991–2020 is the current set; ECCC also publishes 1981–2010 and earlier periods back to 1931–1960

entries.bodyCa: Weather agencies update normals each decade: Environment and Climate Change Canada's current set covers 1991–2020. Calculators and audit reports use them for typical heating and cooling degree-days, so one unusual year doesn't skew the estimate. Some Canadian figures still come from the older 1981–2010 normals.
entries.bodyUs: Weather agencies update normals each decade: NOAA's current US set covers 1991–2020. Calculators and audit reports use them for typical heating and cooling degree days, so one unusual year doesn't skew the estimate.

entries.short: The US weather and climate agency; its National Centers for Environmental Information publish the climate normals and degree-days used for US cities.
entries.body: NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) compile weather station records, many of them at airports, into the 1991–2020 U.S. Climate Normals. These give typical heating and cooling degree-days, temperatures and precipitation for thousands of stations.
entries.whyItMatters: A city's heating and cooling degree-days come from NOAA normals, which is how a page knows whether heating or cooling matters more there.
